Risk Title: Rising water scarcity in Iran leads to a deterioration in health, food security, and livelihood needs
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
Iran’s current water crisis is expected to worsen, with warnings that Tehran could face severe water shortages affecting large parts of the city by October 2025 if water consumption is not drastically reduced. The country has endured a five-year drought, and reservoirs supplying major cities have fallen to their lowest levels in a century. In Tehran, key reservoirs dropped to roughly 14% capacity during peak heat periods, causing widespread water service cuts and outages lasting 12–18 hours in some districts.
Critically low reservoir levels have also hampered hydroelectric power generation, aggravating electricity shortages already driven by fuel constraints and extreme heat. Between June–August, temperatures exceeding 50° C in provinces including Khuzestan, Sistan-Baluchestan, and Yazd led to power and water outages disrupting cooling systems, medical facilities, and water pumping networks. Hospitals report difficulties in maintaining refrigeration for medicines and stable operations during rolling blackouts. At the same time, heat-related mortality has spiked among vulnerable populations, particularly older and displaced people, highlighting severe strain on public health infrastructure. Waterborne disease outbreaks are becoming increasingly likely as water quality deteriorates and sanitation systems falter.
As water scarcity and livelihood pressures intensify, affected populations are likely to seek opportunities in neighbouring countries, including Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, and Türkiye. Political tensions and security concerns may increase irregular migration flows, further aggravating humanitarian needs for displaced people.
Recurrent protests across Fars, Isfahan, and Khuzestan over water and electricity shortages also signal eroding public patience and raise the risk of broader civil unrest amid mounting climate pressures and governance challenges.
([Stimpson 26/03/2025](https://www.stimson.org/2025/no-easy-solutions-for-irans-water-shortages-and-power-outages/), [DW 19/06/2024](https://www.dw.com/en/irans-water-crisis-leads-to-alarming-ground-collapse/a-69405927), [Middle East 18/04/2025](https://middleeast.observer/iran/article/4073/ ), [NCRI 13/08/2025](https://www.ncr-iran.org/en/news/economy/why-iran-is-running-out-of-water-power-and-patience/), [KUNC 17/08/2025](https://www.kunc.org/2025-08-17/iranian-officials-warn-tehran-could-run-out-of-water-in-weeks-amidst-massive-drought),  [Thomson Reuters 17/08/2025](https://www.context.news/climate-risks/opinion/irans-water-crisis-is-driven-by-bad-policies-but-tech-can-help))

By 23 August, storage in Tehran’s five main reservoirs had fallen to 26%, down from around 30% at the beginning of summer and approximately 220 million m³ below the ideal level. Tehran is experiencing its sixth consecutive drought year, with rainfall below 175mm compared with around 280mm needed to restore water conditions. Separately, several villages on Qeshm Island experienced prolonged interruptions to piped water after US strikes damaged desalination infrastructure, demonstrating water supply disruption through environmental and infrastructure-related pathways. Title: Prolonged Drought and Heatwaves
Description: 
Iran’s worsening water crisis is being driven by prolonged drought and intensifying heatwaves, which have sharply reduced rainfall, surface water, and groundwater reserves. Between October 2024 and March 2025, precipitation declined by 41% below long-term averages and 21% compared to the previous year, severely limiting inflows into dams and reservoirs.
The deficit now affects 30 of 31 provinces, with the harshest shortfalls recorded in Hormozgan (–75.9%), Sistan-Baluchestan (–75.4%), and East Azerbaijan (–60%). Record-breaking heat has accelerated evaporation, compounding the depletion of already scarce supplies. In Tehran, key reservoirs, Latian, Lar, Mamloo, and Amir Kabir, have dropped to just 5–12% capacity, with the Lar dam nearly empty, threatening water security and essential urban services.
The combined effects of persistent drought, extreme heat, and excessive groundwater extraction have disrupted Iran’s hydrological balance, leading to land subsidence, reduced agricultural output, and growing food insecurity. These climatic pressures are central triggers of Iran’s water crisis, exacerbating structural weaknesses in governance, infrastructure, and livelihoods.

Title: Climate Change Amplification
Description: 
Climate change is a major amplifier of Iran’s water crisis, intensifying droughts, heatwaves, and rainfall variability across much of the country. Rising temperatures have accelerated evaporation and reduced snowpack in key mountain ranges, diminishing surface runoff that feeds rivers and reservoirs. Over the past two decades, Iran’s average temperature has increased by more than 1.5°C, with extreme heat events becoming longer and more frequent.
This climatic shift has disrupted traditional rainfall cycles, concentrating precipitation into shorter, more intense bursts that fail to replenish groundwater or sustain agriculture. As a result, 30 of 31 provinces now face chronic water stress, with southern and central regions, such as Khuzestan, Yazd, and Sistan-Baluchestan, experiencing the most severe shortages.
Higher temperatures also drive surging demand for irrigation and domestic consumption, compounding existing overuse of groundwater and depletion of reservoirs. The resulting imbalance has caused widespread subsidence, declining crop yields, and rural displacement.

Risk Title: The US/Israel–Iran escalation affecting the Strait of Hormuz drives conflict, food insecurity, livelihood collapse, and protection risks in Iraq
Rationale:
A US–Iran confrontation triggered by a ten-day ultimatum issued by the US administration for Iran to reach a nuclear and regional agreement (placing a potential military trigger in late February or early March 2026) could increase humanitarian needs in Iraq through two compounding mechanisms: direct Iranian proxy escalation via the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) and broader regional economic disruption, including potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Following the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in Syria and Israel's weakening of Hezbollah in Lebanon and Syria, Iraq has become a significant regional asset for Iran. The PMF, an official Iraqi security institution composed largely of Iran-backed militias, represents Iran's likely vector for retaliation against US interests in Iraq. Kata'ib Hezbollah, the largest militia within the PMF, has publicly warned of military response if Iran is attacked.
Iraq's political trajectory compounds this risk. Government formation remains contested between the US administration and Iraq's Coordination Framework over the composition of leadership, with the Trump administration threatening to cut Iraq off from its oil revenues if a candidate closely aligned with Iran and the PMF assumes the premiership. Sitting Prime Minister Al Sudani actively restrained the PMF during the June 2025 Iran–Israel conflict, but a pro-Iran administration would significantly increase militia escalation risk. Political instability, combined with PMF escalation, would likely worsen conditions for Iraq's approximately one million IDPs and deepen sectarian tensions.
Beyond direct proxy conflict, a US–Iran confrontation could trigger humanitarian needs through economic disruption. Prior to the escalation, over 90% of Iraq's oil was exported through the Strait of Hormuz, with the remaining oil exported through the currently closed Ceyhan pipeline connected to Türkiye via Iraq's autonomous Kurdish region. Rationale:
Côte d’Ivoire is preparing for presidential elections scheduled for 25 October 2025. Although recent elections have been relatively peaceful, the political environment is becoming increasingly tense. The Independent Electoral Commission (CEI) released the final electoral roll on 4 June, confirming the exclusion of four prominent opposition leaders: Laurent Gbagbo, Tidjane Thiam, Charles Blé Goudé, and Guillaume Soro. While Thiam was excluded based on nationality concerns, the others were barred because of past judicial convictions. All four are also prohibited from voting.
The exclusion of these high-profile figures has triggered strong criticism from their parties, which have withdrawn from the CEI and denounced a lack of institutional independence. Some, such as Thiam and his party, have appealed to international bodies such as the UNHRC. Others, including former first lady Simone Gbagbo, have warned that the conditions are not in place for peaceful elections. Some parties have announced protests, and public calls for boycotts or civil disobedience could escalate in the coming months.
The memory of the 2010–2011 post-electoral crisis, which caused over 3,000 civilian deaths, still shapes public perception. While today’s situation differs—institutions are more stable, and international scrutiny is higher—the exclusionary political landscape and growing polarisation echo the warning signs of past unrest. The delayed announcement of President Ouattara’s candidacy adds further uncertainty. If he decides to run for a fourth term, in potential breach of constitutional limits, it could become a flashpoint. Risk Title: The expansion of armed groups from central Sahel to coastal countries (Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Togo) leads to displacement and increased food insecurity.
Rationale:
This risk is materialising at a slow pace. A progressive deterioration of the security situation in the northern regions of West African coastal countries is observed. Between October 2022 and January 2023, more than 73 violent incidents involving mostly non-state armed groups have been reported in the northern regions of Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Togo. On the same period in 2022, around 30 incidents were reported. These incidents included attacks on civilians and security forces, kidnappings, the destruction of property, and the use of improvised explosive devices. Benin is the country recording the highest number of attacks by armed groups, followed by Togo. In Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, the attacks are on a smaller scale given a still-low presence of armed groups, but these are becoming more regular. 
The violence has started to trigger internal displacement in Benin and Togo. In Benin, at least 1,200 IDPs have been reported in the department of Atakora, while in Togo, more than 2,200 IDPs are registered in the region of Savanes.  Armed group activity in the northern regions of Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Togo has not seemed to affect food insecurity levels, as the number of food-insecure people remained stable between October–December 2022 compared to the same period in 2021.

Risk Title: Intensifying humanitarian and security crisis in Kenya worsens conditions in refugee camps
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
Kenya’s refugee camps, particularly Dadaab and Kakuma, are facing an increasingly fragile situation owing to severe underfunding, overstretched infrastructure, and surging new arrivals. Cuts in humanitarian aid have already led to reductions in food rations, the closure of essential services, and growing frustration among both refugees and host communities. In 2025, WFP was only able to provide 60% of the minimum food basket by midyear, with responders reporting critical gaps in healthcare, education, and WASH services. The camps, which host more than 600,000 refugees, are still absorbing new displacements from conflict-affected areas of Ethiopia, Somalia, and Sudan. These arrivals further strain already limited resources and contribute to tensions over land, water, and security. Escalating tensions have already led to ethnic clashes, protests, and police interventions within camps including Kakuma and Dadaab. Without urgent interventions, the situation risks spiralling into a protracted crisis marked by localised violence, cross-border insecurity, or forced returns, particularly in light of Kenya's shifting asylum policies and security stance in border regions.
Gaps in healthcare access are increasing the risk of disease outbreaks, particularly as overcrowded living conditions and limited water supplies worsen. Economic hardship and congested settlements are also heightening protection concerns, including gender-based violence. As services and water availability decline, households are expected to relocate within or between camps in search of support, further straining space and social cohesion.
Kenya’s Shirika Plan also continues to face implementation hurdles and growing scepticism among host communities related to resource competition and security. There are concerns that the plan will only benefit those already with resources (business owners and skilled people) rather than the most vulnerable. Given that, the situation may evolve into a sustained protection and humanitarian crisis marked by deteriorating health conditions, rising insecurity, and the potential for forced or premature returns. Refugees may increasingly move outside formal camps in search of livelihoods or better services, often without documentation or assistance. This trend could heighten risks of exploitation, detention, or deportation and further complicate humanitarian coordination and protection efforts. ([TNH 23/05/2025](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2025/05/23/dadaab-voices-what-aid-cuts-mean-kenyas-refugees), [AJ 20/07/2025](https://liberties.aljazeera.com/en/refugees-in-kenya-face-deepening-hunger-as-aid-cuts-bite/)
Hazard materialisation: Kenya’s humanitarian and security situation deteriorates, particularly in refugee-hosting areas such as Garissa and Turkana counties. This systemic breakdown in assistance created a volatile environment, heightening tensions between refugees and host communities, and sparking protests and violent clashes, such as those in Kalobeyei in late June 2025. At the same time, rising insecurity, resource scarcity, and disease outbreaks including dengue fever in Dadaab have compounded the fragility of the camps.

Risk Title: Forecast El Niño conditions threaten crop production and worsen food insecurity in Kenya
Rationale:
El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a 61% probability of El Niño from May–July, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts below-normal June–September (JJAS) rainfall across western and northern Kenya alongside above-normal temperatures nationwide, closely resembling the 2023 El Niño, when below-normal JJAS rainfall affected western Kenya.
The forecast threatens Kenya's principal food-producing areas during a critical stage of the long rains season. Over 70% of the country's annual crop production depends on the long rains, which extend into August–September in the North Rift and western Kenya. These areas had already recorded below-average rainfall in April and early May despite favourable national rainfall totals. Combined with delayed fertiliser deliveries, below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures from June–September are likely to reduce yields of maize, beans, sorghum, and sweet potato, resulting in a below-average October–November harvest.
In northern and eastern pastoral areas, above-average temperatures during the June–September dry season are expected to accelerate the deterioration of rangeland and water resources. Recovery remains fragile after the 2020–2023 drought and the 2023–2024 floods, with depleted herd sizes, persistent livestock disease, and reduced vaccination programmes limiting resilience.
The deteriorating production outlook comes as maize and bean prices remain 6–21% and 8–17% above the five-year average, respectively, driven by depleted household stocks following the poor 2025 short rains, high transport costs, and strong market demand. High household debt further constrains purchasing power. A below-average harvest would tighten domestic food supplies, drive prices higher, and further reduce incomes and food access for farming and pastoral households. Risk Title: A rising number of Syrian refugees opt for an unsafe return to Syria to avoid a deepening economic crisis in Lebanon and the repercussions of the 2020 Beirut explosion
Rationale:
Inflation, rising prices, and the depreciation of the Lebanese lira threaten the livelihoods of Syrian refugees, who struggle to survive on cash assistance (delivered in Lebanese liras) or receive low to no salary from their employers in the informal sector. Because of these factors, as well as Lebanese governmental policies on return, an increasing number of refugees might opt for an unsafe return to Syria.

While the severity of people’s needs has worsened, during 2020, the number of voluntary refugees returning to Syria was only 9,351 – half of the figure registered in 2019. The refugees' decisions to return to Syria were influenced mainly by the security and safety situation, economic growth, public service availability, and personal relationships in their place of origin, while refugees’ poor living conditions in Lebanon were less likely to be an influence. Unless the situation significantly improves in Syria, refugees are unlikely to return.

The 27 November 2024 ceasefire agreement included implementing UNSC Resolution 1701, requiring Hezbollah’s withdrawal from south of the Litani River and blocking arms transfers to the group. The resolution also strengthens the role of the Lebanese Armed Forces and UNIFIL in southern Lebanon, which Hezbollah sees as an effort to weaken its military role.
The deadline for Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon was on 18 February 2025, but their troops continue to occupy five border areas. Despite the ceasefire, Israeli air space violations and air strikes continue, resulting in casualties. The Lebanese army has not responded, leaving civilians in southern Lebanon (mostly the Shia community) without protection. Hezbollah is not retaliating, likely because of its commitment to the ceasefire and challenges in smuggling arms from Iran, signalling a possible weakening of the group.
Lebanon’s Shia community, which makes up around 30% of the population, is growing increasingly frustrated with the Government and the Lebanese Armed Forces for failing to prevent Israeli attacks. Many believe that the Government is deliberately weakening Hezbollah, preventing it from protecting the Shia community. Frustration is likely to lead to more protests, such as those on 14–15 February 2025, after the Government blocked Iranian planes from landing in Beirut in response to Israeli threats. Risk Title: Intercommunal tensions between IDPs and host communities in Lebanon result in localised clashes and further displacement
Rationale:
Rising intercommunal tensions between host communities and IDPs in Lebanon have intensified by late March 2026 amid large-scale displacement and mounting socioeconomic pressure. The re-escalation of hostilities between Hezbollah and Israel since 1 March has displaced an estimated 1.2 million people, mostly from southern Lebanon.
Reports indicate growing host community fatigue, with increasing complaints over overcrowding, pressure on basic services, and the repurposing of schools and public buildings into collective shelters, disrupting education and raising concerns over some IDP sites becoming permanent sites rather than temporary ones.
Besides the high number of IDPs, many other factors drive the tensions, including economic deterioration, rising fuel and commodity prices, and a highly polarised information environment that is fuelling sectarian tensions between Shia and Christian/Sunni populations. Misinformation, especially on social media, including security-related rumours and anti-IDP rhetoric are fuelling tensions. Host communities also express security concerns, fearing that the presence of IDPs may expose their areas to Israeli air strikes. Already, OCHA has reported instances of intercommunal tensions within host communities, although their nature is unclear.
Further escalation may emerge from additional waves of displacement, the expansion of Israeli military operations in southern Lebanon, and Israeli air strikes on areas considered ‘safe’ for IDPs. For example, between 12–13 March 2026, Israeli air strikes expanded into residential areas hosting IDPs in Beirut and Mount Lebanon, killing at least eight people and injuring several others. Such attacks on what is perceived as ‘safe areas’ are heightening tensions between host communities and IDPs.
These dynamics are likely to translate into localised clashes over the next three to six months as displacement continues, particularly in high-density urban areas where resources are scarce and governance is weak. Clashes are most likely between host community residents and IDPs (the majority of whom are Shia) but may also involve civic authorities or security forces enforcing restrictive measures. Such clashes are likely to increase insecurity and fatalities and drive further displacement, particularly for already displaced populations. The risk is assessed as Medium, as key triggers, including large-scale displacement, host community pressure, and rising anti-IDP rhetoric are already present, and recent incidents indicate increasing tensions; however, while widespread intercommunal violence is unlikely, the probability of localised incidents remains significant. ([UNDP 30/03/2026](https://admin.tms-lebanon.com/StaticFiles/Files/TMS_Tensions_Pulse_-_30_March_2026.pdf), [UNHCR 30/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/middle-east-situation-lebanon-flash-update-4-23-29-march-2026), [Megaphone 30/03/2026](https://megaphone.news/oped/%D9%87%D9%84-%D9%85%D8%A7-%D8%B2%D8%A7%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%84%D8%AF-%D9%85%D9%85%D9%83%D9%86%D8%A7), [OCHA 21/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-flash-update-10-escalation-hostilities-lebanon-19-march-2026), [IM Lebanon 13/03/2026](https://www.imlebanon.org/2026/03/13/lebanon-1389/))

Risk Title: Russia's increased military presence in eastern Libya leads to a return to conflict, displacement, and increased humanitarian needs
Rationale:
On 18 December 2024, Russia transferred approximately 1,000 military personnel, including former Syrian soldiers, from Hmeimim airbase in Lattakia governorate in Syria to Benghazi airport in Libya, which is under the control of the Haftar Affiliated Forces. The personnel included officers from Syria’s 5th Corps and 25th Special Tasks Division, along with dismantled S-400 air defence systems. The move appears to be Russia’s strategic aim to strengthen its military presence in Libya, a key asset for its operations in Africa and the Mediterranean. It is also likely an opportunity to compensate for the loss that Russia experienced in Syria following the fall of Bashar Al Assad regime on 8 December.

Risk Title: A contested April 2026 electoral process in Libya heightens localised armed clashes, displacement, and service disruptions
Rationale:
Amid a stalled UN-backed political process and deep institutional fragmentation, political tensions in Libya will likely increase over the next three to six months around the April 2026 presidential and parliamentary elections and ensuing impacts.
The immediate political context is marked by institutional paralysis. Disputes between the east-based House of Representatives (HoR) and the Tripoli-based High Council of State (HCS) over the reconstitution of the High National Election Commission (HNEC) board have stalled the electoral timeline. On 29 December 2025, the HoR voted to fill vacant HNEC board seats, prompting the HCS head to accuse the HoR speaker of violating the UN-backed political agreement. On 5 January 2026, the HCS elected a new HNEC president, triggering objections from eastern authorities. UNSMIL publicly warned on 6 January that these escalatory steps risk undermining the political process. By mid-February, UNSMIL reported “no meaningful progress” on agreeing to election rules or forming a unified Government.
Several triggers could spark election-related violence. First, unilateral actions by either side on electoral institutions or rules risk provoking armed responses from rival authorities and affiliated militias. Second, the proposed UNSMIL structured dialogue risks reinforcing existing power imbalances, particularly if perceived as bypassing key stakeholders or legitimising contested authorities. Third, rising economic pressure – including fuel shortages, declining living standards, and the devaluation of the Libyan dinar by nearly 15% on 18 January – is deepening public frustration. Fourth, escalating security incidents and assassinations are heightening tensions. Most notably, the killing of Saif al-Islam Gaddafi on 3 February, followed by a prosecutor-led investigation announced on 5 February without visible accountability measures, may reinforce perceptions that armed groups can carry out political violence with impunity, contributing to heightened tensions and fears of politically motivated targeting.
If violence erupts, it will most likely take the form of localised armed clashes between rival armed groups aligned with eastern and western authorities instead of conflict on nationwide front lines. High-risk areas include Tripoli and its surroundings, where competing militias operate; Benghazi city and eastern Libya, where tensions between political authorities and security forces persist; and southern border areas, where armed groups and criminal networks are active. Violence could include targeted killings, attacks on electoral institutions, the intimidation of political figures, and clashes over strategic infrastructure. Given Libya’s history, even limited clashes could trigger localised displacement, disrupt basic services, and restrict humanitarian access, particularly in urban centres and contested southern regions.
Regional involvement, including Tunisia’s February proposal with Algeria and Egypt in coordination with UNSMIL, may help reduce tensions by supporting a Libyan-led dialogue. Without agreement among Libyan authorities and armed groups, however, it is unlikely to prevent election-related violence. Risk Title: El Niño drives drought conditions, increasing food insecurity and heightening humanitarian needs in Madagascar in 2027
Rationale: Current models indicate a very high probability for El Niño to develop by July 2026 and persist into early 2027. In Madagascar, El Niño typically drives precipitation and temperature anomalies, with dry conditions in southern parts of the country and heavy rainfall in the north and east. In 2015–2016 and 2023–2024, El Niño caused prolonged drought conditions and crop failure, resulting in increased food insecurity that particularly affected the country's south. Seasonal forecasts anticipate near-average precipitation in July–September and below-average precipitation across most of the country in October–December. The same forecasts indicate a very high probability of above-average temperatures across the entire country in July–December. Drier and hotter-than-average conditions may affect the start of the rainy season, which runs October–April and is essential for producing Madagascar's main staple cereals, such as maize and rice, harvested in April–June. This may lead to below-average yields, with severe consequences for the population's access to food in 2027, widening food consumption gaps and increasing malnutrition rates. Impacts may also extend to other staple crops, such as cassava, beans, and sweet potatoes, as well as to agricultural labour availability, which usually peaks between November–March. Limited rainfall and abnormally high temperatures may also reduce pasture availability, resulting in deteriorating livestock body conditions and increased morbidity and mortality. Dry conditions are also likely to affect access to water for domestic consumption, potentially leading to reliance on unsafe water sources and limiting hygiene and sanitation practices. These combined effects are expected to increase humanitarian needs, strain local coping mechanisms, and heighten dependence on external assistance, particularly among rural households already vulnerable to climate variability. The country shows a high pre-existing vulnerability to climatic shocks, including reliance on rainfed agriculture, limited water and sanitation infrastructure, and low coping capacity. Current vulnerability / Coping capacitie: Madagascar faces high structural vulnerability, with extreme poverty estimated at around 65% in April 2026, limiting households' ability to absorb shocks. Livelihoods are largely dependent on rainfed agriculture, making them highly sensitive to climate variability. Recurrent climatic shocks continue to erode resilience, as demonstrated by the cyclones Fytia and Gezani in early 2026, which affected nearly 700,000 people, damaging homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods. Food security conditions remain fragile. During the February–April 2026 period, an estimated 1.8 million people were expected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes, with limited access to food and income. In southwestern Madagascar, persistent rainfall shortages since the start of the rainy season in October 2025 have limited agricultural production. Field assessments conducted in early May 2026 confirmed maize and pulse yields below average for the typical May harvest period. Local markets also showed unusually low supplies of maize and cassava. Coping capacity is further constrained by worsening malnutrition levels, with around 558,000 children under five either affected or at risk of acute malnutrition between May 2025 and April 2026. Many households are already employing coping mechanisms with potentially harmful consequences, including reducing food intake, selling productive assets, or taking on debt. Repeated exposure to shocks, combined with limited access to services and weak infrastructure, continues to reduce households' ability to recover, increasing dependence on humanitarian assistance. Expected impact: The effects of El Niño-induced drought are expected to result in deteriorating food security, increased malnutrition, and heightened humanitarian needs. In the south, rainfall deficits are likely to lead to the most severe impacts, as the region already experiences prolonged dry conditions and a poor 2025–2026 rainy season. Across the country, similarly poor conditions in 2026–2027 may lead to reduced agricultural production, depletion of household food stocks, and increased reliance on markets, where purchasing power remains constrained because of poverty and limited income opportunities. This is expected to widen food consumption gaps, particularly among rural households dependent on rainfed agriculture. El Niño is also expected to significantly affect WASH conditions and public health. In southern areas, water scarcity will likely reduce access to safe drinking water and hygiene services. Poor WASH access already contributes significantly to child mortality and illness. Across affected areas, pre-existing vulnerabilities such as high poverty, limited coping capacity, and weak infrastructure are likely to amplify the impact of these shocks. Malnutrition risks are expected to increase, particularly among children under five, driven by reduced food availability and access and deteriorated access to water, sanitation, and hygiene. At the same time, repeated shocks are likely to further erode households' coping strategies, pushing them to adopt coping mechanisms with potentially harmful consequences, including reducing food intake and selling productive assets. Risk Title: Deterioration of humanitarian situation in Mali
Rationale: On 18 August, troops in Bamako conducted a mutiny and arrested the country's president, Ibrahim Boubacar Keita, and vice-president. Late in the night between 18-19 August, IBK resigned dissolving the parliament and the government. Men claiming to be the spokespeople of the "National Committe for the Salvation of the People" gave an address on the country's public TV station where they announced that the country's borders were now closed and a curfew was in place. They also promised that the Malian armed forces would honour all of their current commitments (G5 Sahel and Barkhane, 2015 peace deal), and that elections would be organized in a "reasonable" amount of time. People have been protesting since a controversial ruling by the country's Constitutional Court flipped 31 legislative seats, including 10 that went to IBK's party. The protests were organized by the M5-RFP coalition under the guidance of Immam Dicko. So far, there is no evidence of coordination between the coup plotters and M5-RFP. The main difference between this coup and the one in 2012, which makes predicting outcomes difficult, is that this time high-ranking officers are involved (The leader is Colonel Assimi Goita). The TV statement also makes it seem like the coup plotters are politically savvy. The coup has drawn international condemnation, including ECOWAS, AU, France, USA and the UN. Consequences so far: ECOWAS has called on their members to close their borders with Mali and stop financial flows. A prolonged dispute between ECOWAS and Mali could mean economic problems for the local population, and access issues for the humanitarian sector. If the coup leads to even lower state and coalition presence in conflict-affected areas, we could see a dramatic rise in violence. As of writing all senarios are plausible. Rainy season is underway, with shifted priorities, humanitarian response could be affected.

Risk Title: Economic sanctions lead to the loss of livelihoods and increased food insecurity.
Rationale: On 9 January 2022 the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) decided to apply several economic sanctions against Mali, including the closure of land and air borders with member countries, the suspension of all commercial and financial transactions between ECOWAS countries and Mali, and the freezing of Malian assets in the Central Banks of ECOWAS. These sanctions were applied in reaction to the decision of the Transition authorities to postpone the presidential election, initially scheduled for February 2022, and following the submission of a timetable for a transition period of five years at the end of the Assises Nationales de la Refondation −consultations with the population with the objective to fix the date of the next elections and to guarantee the return of civilians to power. The five-year period was judged too long by ECOWAS.
Hazard materialisation: This risk has partially materialised. The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) economic sanctions against Mali were lifted on 3 July 2022 after the junta presented a timetable for the next presidential elections, which it set for March 2024. The individual sanctions against the leaders of the junta and the suspension of Mali from the organs of ECOWAS remain until the return of civilian power in the country.
Current vulnerability / Coping capacitie: 1.2 million people are already facing a food crisis. The sanctions will further reduce their ability to access to food.
Expected impact: These sanctions are likely to cause loss of livelihoods and increased food insecurity, aggravated by the persistent conflict and the economic consequences of COVID-19, including difficulties in the supply of food products and agricultural inputs, rising prices, and job losses (IRC 19/01/2022). Even though the authorities try to resort to other neighboring non-ECOWAS countries to circumvent the effects of the sanctions, the transport of essential goods that are exempt from the sanctions will likely be disrupted due to the increase in border controls by neighbouring countries (Le Point 14/01/2022). Border closure with neighboring countries such as Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire will primarily affect the cotton and gold sectors, which are Mali's main export products (The Guardian 28/01/2022; African Business 14/01/2022; Jeune Afrique 31/01/2022). The decrease in customs revenue due to the reduction in imports while the country can no longer borrow money from regional financial institutions could lead to a lack of cash once the state reserves are exhausted. The salaries of civil servants and the military may therefore not be paid in the coming months (Le Point 14/01/2022). As during the 2020 sanctions, remittances, on which many households depend for their survival are likely to become impossible due to the lack of cash (Le Monde 25/09/2020). Capping withdrawals and stopping the granting of new credit will greatly reduce the coping capacity of those affected (DW 24/09/2020).
Impact materialisation description: This risk has partially materialised in terms of rising food prices, but the impact of sanctions on humanitarian access has been very limited. The same can be said for the impact of sanctions on livestock farming. The increase in food insecurity has materialised, but food security was expected to deteriorate nationwide regardless of the sanctions, making it difficult to attribute solely to the economic sanctions that lasted almost six months. The decline in trade flows with external markets in connection with ECOWAS sanctions has increased food prices, which continue to be high. Poor households have seen their access to food deteriorate further.

Risk Title: Failure of essential services owing to the blockade in Mali leads to civil unrest and destabilisation and aggravates needs
Risk Type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
Rationale:
Since September 2025, Jama'a Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an Al Qaeda–affiliated group, has expanded its blockade strategy from the traditional conflict zones in northern and central Mali (Gao, Mopti, Tombouctou) to southern and southwestern regions, including Kayes, Koulikoro, and Ségou. This expansion signals a shift towards a strategy of coercive governance, with JNIM using economic strangulation – via targeted attacks on fuel convoys and the imposition of checkpoints along critical trade routes – to undermine state legitimacy and force power-sharing negotiations. The blockade marks the first large-scale attempt to encircle Bamako, Mali’s capital, and demonstrates the group’s increasing operational reach.
The blockades have resulted in acute shortages of fuel, electricity, and essential goods across the country. Fuel prices in Bamako surged by over 400% in October, with queues lasting hours and some car owners abandoning vehicles at petrol stations. Major public services, including health and education, have been severely disrupted. The Government closed schools and universities nationwide from 27 October to 9 November, citing the inability of staff and students to reach facilities amid the fuel crisis. Power cuts have intensified, and hospitals in peripheral cities, such as Sikasso and Koutiala, have reported severely limited operations. JNIM has enforced the blockade by destroying an estimated 200 fuel tankers since September, as well as killing at least 15 drivers and abducting others. The group has openly threatened transporters and companies attempting to defy the blockade. Humanitarian responders report that key corridors – particularly those linking Mali to Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire – are patrolled through armed checkpoints, and the Government is unable to maintain secure access despite military escorts. Several areas, such as Loulouni in the south and towns in Mopti and Gao, remain fully or partially isolated.
The humanitarian situation is likely to deteriorate further as a result of the blockade. Food insecurity, protection risks – particularly for women and girls – and displacement are expected to worsen amid prolonged service collapse. The blockades are likely to further destabilise Mali by directly undermining state authority and creating conditions for civil unrest. The fuel crisis caused by the blockade has led to the disruption of essential services, such as electricity, healthcare, water, and transportation, which are crucial for state legitimacy. Risk Title: Continued coordinated JNIM–FLA attacks and blockades increase protection risks, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints in Mali
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
Since late April 2026, the unprecedented operational coordination between Jama’at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de libération de l’Azawad (FLA) has significantly increased pressure on Mali’s security apparatus and exposed vulnerabilities in state control across northern, central, and western regions. Over the next one to three months, three converging escalation dynamics will likely worsen humanitarian conditions significantly across Mali. The assassination of Defence Minister Gen. Sadio Camara on 25 April 2026 created a command vacuum in Mali's security apparatus leadership. As the junta’s chief military strategist and the primary architect of the partnership with Russia’s Africa Corps, his death is likely to severely hamper coordination of counter-offensive operations, make Malian-Russian tactical responses less cohesive, and embolden further advances by armed groups at a critical juncture of territorial contestation.

JNIM and the FLA are both targeting urban supply chains, favouring economic attrition strategies over military objectives. With the FLA explicitly signalling southward expansion following the capture of Kidal region, citing Gao and Tombouctou as its next targets, and JNIM threatening a full blockade of Bamako region along the Senegalese and Ivorian corridors, populations in major urban centres face mounting risks of acute fuel and food shortages. Critically low stocks in the capital mean any sustained suspension of truck traffic could rapidly disrupt electricity, healthcare, and water access for millions already living under severe humanitarian stress. Towns such as Bandiagara and Douentza are already becoming more isolated because of road insecurity and flight suspensions, significantly constraining humanitarian access and the movement of goods and people.

Rationale:
As of July 2025, pressure over limited resources continues to increase, especially in Hodh Ech Chargui wilaya, where the number of Malian refugees continues to increase, while drought and seasonal dry conditions continue in depletion of water and grazing resources, which may trigger tensions and localized clashes. 
The southeastern Hodh Chargui wilaya, which borders Mali, now hosts over 160,000 Malian refugees as of 30 June 2025, compromising over 25.5% of the total population of the wilaya, up from 19% in 2024. The refugee-to-host population ratio in some areas exceeds 1:4, straining access to local sources of water, fuel wood, and grazing land. Competition for scarce water, land, and grazing resources is intensifying between refugees, local communities, and Mauritanian returnees, who were previously displaced from Mali due to insecurity and violence. Localised tensions over access to farmland and grazing areas are often reported and is likely, as was the case in 2022 following a large influx of Malian refugees into Mauritania. Simultaneously, recurring climate shocks such as prolonged droughts, which have affected the country for several decades, and floods in 2024, which displaced 1,125 people and caused damage to agriculture and grazing areas, have weakened rural livelihoods, especially in agropastoral areas where over 60% of the population depends on rain-fed agriculture and livestock.
If refugee flows from Mali continue or host resources become further depleted, social cohesion could be further disrupted, triggering localised clashes between communities over land, water, and grazing access. Departments such as Bassikounou, Fassala, and Amourj, that host the highest Malian refugees population and where land tenure is contested between returnees and local families, are likely to report localised clashes. Risk Title: Dzud-related extreme weather conditions leading to decreased livelihoods.
Rationale:
The “dzud” is a multiple natural disaster comprising summer drought resulting in inadequate pasture and production of hay, followed by severe winter conditions consisting heavy snow cover, winds, and lower-than-normal temperatures. The phenomenon prevents livestock from accessing pasture or from receiving adequate hay and fodder, resulting in high mortality levels, especially in steppe (dry and grassy plain), vast grassland, devoid of trees and with little diversity in vegetation.

The frequency of severe winters has doubled in the past 20 years, making only 1% of the steppe suitable for growing crops. These conditions are commonly preceded by a dry summer with equally scant grazing.  Livestock struggle to build up the stores of fat they need for winter, and farming families risk losing their main source of income. A quarter to a third of the national herd population were lost in the past two dzud events.

According to the National Agency for Meteorology and Environmental Monitoring, around 15% of the Mongolian territory is at the highest level of risk (extreme risk) and around 45% is at high level of dzud risk in 2023.

The usual peak period for livestock mortality is February to April. December through February are the coldest months of the year, when livestock lose most of their fat and become malnourished. Assessments identified the period January to April 2023 to be the critical period to act early and protect herder livelihoods.
Hazard materialisation: As of 1 February, approximately 70% of Mongolia or a total of 22 Aimags or provinces and 310 Soums or townships, are at either high or extreme Dzud situation.

Risk Title: Escalating civil unrest leads to increased protection risks and poverty
Rationale:
On 9 October 2024, Mozambique held general elections featuring three main presidential candidates: the Frelimo party’s Daniel Chapo, successor to outgoing President Filipe Nyusi; Venâncio Mondlane of the new Podemos party; and Ossufo Momade of the Renamo party.  Allegations of vote tampering, restricted access for opposition representatives and observers, 
and the misuse of state resources marred the election process  Though Chapo led early results, Mondlane alleged victory on 
10 October based on parallel vote counts.
On 21 October, protests erupted after Mondlane called for demonstrations and a nationwide general strike. The police’s heavy-handed response – including firing live ammunition at demonstrators; the targeted killing of two senior opposition figures, including  Mondlane’s lawyer, who was preparing a case claiming electoral fraud; and the declaration by the National Election Commission on 24 October of Chapo as the winner with 71% of the votes– intensified the protests across the country, including in Beira, Maputo, Nacala,  Pemba, Nampula, Zambezia, and Chimoio. Mondlane subsequently went into hiding, 
although he has continued to incite protesters, through social media, promising to continue until the Frelimo party concedes the election. 
Between 21 October and 13 December, 275 protests and riots were reported, with at least 130 people killed, more than 2,000 injured (including by bullets), and almost 4,000 arrested and detained, including children. Protests have grown violent in urban centres, such as Maputo, Nampula, and Zambezia, 
evidenced by the increasing number of casualties, arrests from the riots, and violent clashes with the police, who have used live ammunition and tear gas. After Cyclone Chido hit northern Mozambique on 15 December, Mondlane called for a temporary halt in the protests to mourn the victims.  According to Mondlane, protests, which will be “life or death”, should restart on 23 December.
Since the protests began, economic disruption has been extensive and continues to worsen as general strikes shut down businesses and block key infrastructure. Protests that cause road closures frequently paralyse urban centres, including Maputo, Nampula, and Zambezia. Between 7–9 December, the state-owned Electricidade de Moçambique announced electricity provision restrictions in the south of the country, including 
Maputo, because of the protests. Until 11 December, operations in Maputo port remained suspended since 6 November, affecting the flow of goods. The border with South Africa has also been temporarily closed on different occasions, most recently between 9–12 December, affecting crucial imports such as food supplies.
Since the start of the protests, government crackdowns on free speech – including mobile network and internet shutdowns, press restrictions, and intimidation – have further fuelled tensions. While foreign governments and human rights organisations condemn the excessive use of force, more opposition parties and figures, including the Renamo party, have joined the call to overturn the elections. Protests have evolved from rejecting alleged election fraud to include broader demands for systemic reform, citing corruption, poverty, a lack of opportunities, and restricted freedoms under the Frelimo party’s decades-long rule.
Over the next one to three months, there is a very high probability of escalating civil unrest across the country, as neither Mondlane nor the Government appears willing to compromise. The unrest could worsen with the expected 23 December annoucement by the Constitutional Council of the verified election results, continued internet shutdowns and press restrictions,  direct incitement to violence or extremism from either side, and increasing violent crackdowns and police brutality. An escalation could damage the economy and lead to a widespread breakdown in law and order, intensifying poverty, aggravating humanitarian needs (such as protection and food security), and further limiting humanitarian access, including for the humanitarian response to Cyclone Chido.

Update 28/02/2025
From 21 October 2024 to 25 February 2025, over 300 deaths related to post-election protests have been reported nationwide. A Mozambican civil society monitoring group indicated that at least seven additional people died in clashes with security forces on 15 January 2025. Maputo province appears to be the most affected area, with more than 100 fatalities documented. There have also been reports of unlawful arrests, detentions, forced disappearances, and injuries.
Despite the absence of substantial post-election demonstrations in February, tensions remain elevated. The initial catalyst for these protests was the controversial outcome of the previous national elections in October 2024, which many deemed fraudulent. That said, the current unrest has evolved, with the cost of living becoming a primary concern. This was evidenced in Inhambane province on 25 February, where protesters violently vandalised and torched the headquarters of Mozambique’s governing Frelimo party. The economy of Mozambique contracted by 4.87% in the fourth quarter of 2024 compared to the same period the previous year as a result of post-election protests.

Update 27/03/2025
As of March 2025, more than 350 people have been killed from the disputed October 2024 elections as the country continues to experience civil unrest and economic challenges.​
On 05 March, Mozambican police fired upon supporters of opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane during a protest march in Maputo, injuring more than 15 people. The demonstrators were protesting ahead of President Daniel Chapo's signing of an agreement with certain political parties aimed at ending months of post-election protests. Mondlane, who was excluded from these negotiations, pledged to continue his protests against the government. However, on 23 March opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane and President Daniel Chapo had a meeting in Maputo and agreed to put an end to the unrest and was part of “the ongoing effort to promote national stability and strengthen the commitment to reconciliation and the unity of Mozambicans.’’
Both parties have agreed to end all forms of violence, including state violence and attacks on members of Frelimo and other groups. Those injured during the post-election protests, including police officers and Frelimo members, will receive free medical care and medication. Families of those killed in the protests will be provided with social assistance and compensation, while psychological support will be available for those affected by the violence. Additionally, detainees arrested in connection with the protests will be granted pardons. To formalize these commitments, teams are being established to draft an official agreement reflecting the consensus reached.
The situation remains volatile, with uncertainty if protests will continue, a heavy-handed security response, and significant economic downturns. Efforts to mediate the crisis have yet to yield substantial results, and the potential for further unrest persists.

Flood damage to informal shelters and services in displacement sites may force repeated or secondary displacement, while reduced access to farmland and markets is likely to intensify food insecurity and negative coping strategies.

Risk Title: El Niño-induced dry conditions in southern and central Mozambique and floods in the northern provinces increase humanitarian needs in 2026 and early 2027
Rationale: Climate projections indicate a high likelihood of El Niño conditions developing in July 2026 and persisting into the 2026/2027 rainy season, coinciding with Mozambique's main agricultural period. El Niño will drive contrasting rainfall patterns, with drier conditions in southern and central regions and wetter conditions in the north. The anticipated event is driven by abnormal warming of equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures, which disrupts global atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. El Niño typically brings below-normal rains in southern Mozambique and above-normal rains to the northern provinces, raising the likelihood of flooding and river overflow. Seasonal forecasts for the October–December period anticipate these typical El Niño patterns, indicating a moderate probability of above-average precipitation in the north and below-average precipitation in the south. The entire country is expected to experience above-average temperatures in July–December, which will compound dry conditions in the south and increase the risk of waterborne and vector-borne diseases in flood-exposed areas. Mozambique's high exposure to climate variability and reliance on rainfed agriculture further amplify vulnerability to climatic shocks. From September–October 2026, delayed or below-average precipitation in southern and central areas, combined with abnormally high temperatures, may affect land preparation and planting. If dry conditions continue through early 2027, crop yields and water availability may decrease, leading to a below-average maize, rice, millet, and sorghum harvest. At the same time, northern areas are likely to experience above-average precipitation, which may be beneficial to agriculture but also increases the risk of flooding, infrastructure damage, and displacement. These combined impacts are expected to increase humanitarian needs, particularly in food security, nutrition, WASH, and health. Islamic State Mozambique (ISM) activity in northern Mozambique has increasingly shifted towards mobile, small-group operations as a response to intensified military pressure from Mozambican security forces and their regional partners. Increased patrols, aerial surveillance, and continued counterinsurgency operations have reduced non-state armed groups' capacity to hold territory. As a result, ISM have increasingly dispersed from areas under intensified military pressure in Macomia district towards southern and western Cabo Delgado province. ISM have moved through Quissanga, Mecufi, and Meluco towards Ancuabe and Chiure districts, while other groups moved west towards Montepuez district and subsequently towards Niassa province. One group also crossed into Erati district in Nampula province.
Over the next six months, continued military pressure in Cabo Delgado is expected to further disperse ISM fighters towards areas with weaker security coverage. Remote forested areas and limited state presence in parts of Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, which have had some pockets of attacks, provide opportunities for small groups to move and conduct more attacks. ISM have increasingly targeted informal gold mining sites for looting and ransom, while attacks on vehicles and road users have generated additional income through extortion. In Niassa, the July–November hunting season also increases the presence of hunting camps, tourism operators, and vehicles in remote areas, creating potential high-value targets for ransom and material gains. If ISM establish a presence in Montepuez, Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, these activities could provide alternative sources of revenue and sustain their operations. ([ACLED 05/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-august-2026), [IOM 24/06/2026](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/mozambique-movement-alert-report-163-24-june-2026), [ACLED 08/09/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-september-2026), [OCHA 08/09/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/mozambique/mozambique-2026-humanitarian-response-conflict-overview-july-2026-enpt), [Gov.UK accessed 22/09/2026](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/mozambique/regional-risks))

Current vulnerability / Coping capacitie:
Northern Mozambique's capacity to absorb new conflict shocks remains constrained by recurrent displacement, limited access to basic services, and restricted humanitarian access. The 2026 humanitarian response plan targets 1.1 million people across 17 districts in Cabo Delgado, two in Nampula, and one in Niassa by the end of July.
Niassa has comparatively lower conflict exposure than Cabo Delgado but has limited security coverage across its vast rural and conservation areas. The September incursion demonstrated the challenge: troops from the Armed Defence Forces of Mozambique deployed along the Lugenda River were unable to prevent an ISM group from entering Niassa and reaching Marrupa.
Expansion through remote rural and forest areas. ISM's ability to move in small groups through poorly secured areas increases the possibility of attacks beyond the established conflict epicentre. The movement of approximately 30 fighters from Lusaka in Montepuez into Marrupa illustrates this pattern.
Repeated cyclone impacts, including Kenneth (2019), Gombe (2022), and Chido (2024), have damaged homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods across Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Niassa, weakening household coping capacities and recovery efforts. This reduces communities' ability to absorb further displacement and livelihood disruptions resulting from insurgent movements. ([ACLED 05/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-august-2026), [IOM 24/06/2026](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/mozambique-movement-alert-report-163-24-june-2026), [ACLED 08/09/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-september-2026), [OCHA 08/09/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/mozambique/mozambique-2026-humanitarian-response-conflict-overview-july-2026-enpt), [EC accessed 22/09/2026](https://civil-protection-humanitarian-aid.ec.europa.eu/where/africa/mozambique_en), [INGD accessed 30/09/2026](https://conceitos.org/projectos/publicos/resilienciaclimatica/index.html), [OCHA 28/01/2025](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/mozambique/mozambique-cabo-delgado-nampula-niassa-humanitarian-snapshot-december-2024-enpt))

Expected impact:
Protection risks are likely to increase through killings, abductions, family separation, property destruction, and restrictions on movement, while further operations by the Armed Defence Forces of Mozambique in newly affected areas could expose civilians to clashes, displacement, and disruption of access to livelihoods and services. The September attack in Marrupa already killed two people, abducted 11, and displaced about 2,700 people. Children face an additional risk of abduction and forced recruitment. Recent recruitment and use of children by non-state armed groups has been documented in northern Mozambique, including the abduction of three children in Cabo Delgado in February 2026.
Livelihoods are likely to deteriorate and food insecurity to increase as violence restricts access to farmland, markets, and labour opportunities. In 2025, Marrupa district, Niassa province, had an estimated 110,000 inhabitants, with smallholder agriculture an important source of food and income. Some households in the district were found to depend entirely on small-scale farming after previous climate shocks. Niassa had about 196,000 people in Crisis or worse (IPC Phase 3+) between October 2025 and March 2026, equivalent to 12% of its analysed population. Further violence, particularly ahead of the November lean season, could reduce household food stocks, interrupt agricultural activity, and increase market dependence. Disruption is particularly important during the July–November hunting season, which represents a critical seasonal driver of formal revenue and local livelihoods. A persistent ISM presence in Niassa may destabilise the local economy, forcing community displacement and restricting access to vital tourism-dependent livelihoods.
Health services could deteriorate if attacks damage facilities or insecurity prevents health workers and communities from reaching them. The Marrupa attack destroyed a health centre, demonstrating that health infrastructure can be directly affected by ISM attacks; this would remove already limited local capacity rather than necessarily indicating deliberate targeting of health services. In 2025, Niassa had 221 health facilities in total. Of these, four were higher-level referral hospitals: three secondary (district/rural/general) and one tertiary (provincial) hospital, while many communities in Mozambique already travel long distances to reach care. Further displacement and road insecurity could therefore interrupt routine, maternal, and child healthcare, as well as vaccination and emergency referrals. Risk Title: Increased violence around upcoming elections in early 2022 leads to civil war and countrywide conflict after the elections
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
The military coup in Myanmar on 1 February resulted in over 750 protesters killed and over 4,000 detained (with reports of torture). An emergency state was originally imposed for a year but was extended until August 2023 with the promise of holding free and fair multi-party elections afterwards. The next elections are likely to pose a threat of escalation into civil war based on anti-coup protests so far, which were violent, and an increase in clashes with ethnic armed groups. If The National Unity Government (NUG) becomes armed, this could escalate into countrywide conflict. United Nations experts already issued concerns about a civil war or a countrywide conflict outbreak. Over 200 NGOs urged the United Nations Security Council to impose an arms embargo on Myanmar. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations urged all parties to end violence.

The People's Defence Force (PDF) was formed by the shadow NUG on 5 May as an anti-junta resistance movement to the 1 February coup. Ethnic armed groups (EAOs) reacted to the coup and violence against protesters by supporting the NUG and the civil disobedience movement, training members and youth for the PDF, and clashing with the army in support of the anti-coup movement.

Risk Title: Conscription policies implemented by the Myanmar military junta and some EAOs heighten protection concerns throughout the country
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
On 10 February 2024, Myanmar’s military junta announced the activation of the conscription law enforcing mandatory military service for young people. Evading conscription could result in a prison sentence.
Around 14 million civilians are eligible for conscription. The annual recruitment target is estimated to be around 50,000 to 70,000 people. The activation of the law is considered a response to the loss of military junta troops through deaths, injuries, desertions, and defections in the armed conflict against armed resistance groups, comprising anti-coup resistance forces and ethnic armed organisations (EAOs). 
Similar conscription has also been observed among some of the EAOs, both against and allied with the military, in northern Shan state, indicating a possible expansion of the warscape in the state. 
It has been widely reported that young people are reluctant to serve in the military under the military junta and some may even join the armed resistance groups instead of the military as, in general, they oppose the military junta. Many other are reported to be reluctant to join any groups that are implementing conscription laws.
There have been reports of people being kidnapped, arrested, or compelled into joining the military and used as human shields in 2023 and 2024. Rohingyas living in the IDP camps of Rakhine state are reportedly a target of the military junta for forced recruitment. There have been reports of people trying to leave the country, especially to Thailand, which has increased the risk of increased refugee influx in Thailand.
Conscription laws implemented by the military junta and some EAOs will likely geographically expand and intensify armed conflict in the country in 2024.

UPDATE (05/01/2025)
Tens of thousands of working-age young people were forcibly recruited in 2024, both by the military junta and anti-military resistance forces. This conscription drive has led to several consequences. It caused a wave of emigration, which adversely affected various industries, particularly agriculture, due to a decrease in employment. Additionally, it prompted numerous domestic companies to leave the country. In Rakhine, conscription of the Rohingya fuelled intercommunal tensions between the Rohingya and the ethnic Rakhine residents. It also contributed to increased early marriages, especially in rural communities. The conscription law is depleting the youth population, which is a driving force of humanitarian action, and has further restricted humanitarian access in the country.

Impact materialisation description:
The military junta and some anti-military resistance forces implemented conscription, leading to fears among many in the country and a significant outflow of people to Thailand. The military regime has enlisted the Rohingya using both compulsion and allurement. It has also backed Rohingya armed groups in their battle against the Arakan Army. Since the December 2025 elections in Myanmar, conflict and protection risks have not decreased but instead remain acute. The elections were widely criticised as neither free nor fair. In contrast, countries such as China and India maintained engagement, reflecting geopolitical divisions over recognition.

Risk Title: Military operations to secure the Dawei Special Economic Zone cause further forced displacement and severe protection risks in Dawei district, Tanintharyi region
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
By 28 August 2026, an estimated 700–1,000 military personnel were conducting clearance operations around the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Yebyu township after a late-June order to protect the strategic projects. Since 9 July, fighting, raids, arson, looting, arbitrary arrests, and killings have displaced more than 4,500 people from eight Nabule villages. Renewed fighting near the SEZ from 21–22 August caused further civilian displacement. More than 2,000 people were displaced from ten villages in Thayetchaung township in August.
The concentration of military deployments around the project area, following orders to protect strategic infrastructure and agreements to revive the project, indicates that the operation is intended to secure the SEZ. The SEZ is a long-stalled port and industrial zone planned to include a deep-sea port, coal-fired power plant, oil refinery, and liquefied natural gas facilities. The risk is more immediate because Myanmar and Russia revived the project in 2025, signed a June 2026 power plant agreement, and included the Dawei port, refinery, and power plant in their August Moscow agreements. Risk Title: Escalation of inter-group conflict between Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and Islamic State Sahel Province in western Niger leads to increased violence against civilians and displacement
Rationale:
In early April 2026, the Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) attacked a Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) position in Tillabéri, marking the first reported direct confrontation between the two groups in Niger after years of rivalry concentrated in Mali and Burkina Faso. Tillabéri is already one of the most affected areas in the central Sahel, where violence against civilians, displacement, and weak state presence have created acute protection risks. Tillabéri recorded the highest level of civilian targeting across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger in 2025, with over 1,200 of Niger’s 1,939 civilian fatalities occurring there, primarily attributed to ISSP, followed by JNIM and the Nigerien military. 
The risk of escalation is linked to the geographic expansion of JNIM–ISSP competition into western Niger, where both groups are increasingly competing for territorial influence, recruitment networks, road axes, and local economies. Recent attacks on military installations in Tahoua city, including the Base Aérienne 401 and the 42nd battalion headquarters in March 2026, indicate that insecurity is increasingly affecting strategic urban and military locations beyond the main rural border areas of Tillabéri. These developments have already disrupted humanitarian operations, with UNHAS flights temporarily suspended because of insecurity and repercussions on humanitarian access. 
Over the next six months, escalation of JNIM–ISSP clashes in western Niger could mirror patterns seen in Mali and Burkina Faso, where rivalry expansion led to heightened violence against civilians, mass displacement, and further erosion of state control. Armed group competition and pressure on key road axes will likely expand attacks into previously less-affected communes and towns in western Niger, leading to a deterioration in civilian security and access to services. Both groups may intensify targeting of populations perceived to support rivals, particularly rural communities in contested border areas of Tillabéri, as well as displaced and host communities, leaving civilians vulnerable to crossfire, accusations of collaboration, and illegal taxation. Tillabéri’s existing high baseline of civilian harm, combined with weak state presence, protracted displacement, and fragile livelihoods, could amplify the impact of further escalation. New displacement, exacerbated food insecurity, and deepened humanitarian access constraints are likely as groups compete for recruitment and resources in this strategic border zone. Risk Title: Lakurawa armed group resurgence in North West Nigeria and southern Niger heightens insecurity and leads to more displacement
Rationale:
Lakurawa is a violent extremist group active in northern Nigeria, with suspected links to the Islamic State – Sahel Province. Originating from herders migrating from Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger in the 2010s, the group initially operated as a criminal gang before evolving into a self-proclaimed protector against banditry. Over time, it has imposed strict religious ideologies and sought territorial control.
In November 2024, Lakurawa launched a deadly attack in Kebbi state, Nigeria, killing at least 15 people. Since then, it has expanded operations into Niger, enforcing taxes, imposing their interpretation of Islamic law, and distributing resources to gain community support. Despite Nigerian military operations, the group remains largely free to operate in Niger, aggravating security gaps along the border.
Its growing alliances with armed groups in the Sahel provide it with external backing, increasing the likelihood of prolonged instability. Heightened tensions with regional bandits, particularly in Sokoto and Kebbi states, could escalate into cycles of retaliatory violence, deepening the crisis and destabilising the region.
Compounding these challenges, poor intelligence and a lack of coordination among security groups have led to conflicting assessments of Lakurawa. While police forces downplay the threat, the military categorises Lakurawa as an ‘emerging terrorist organisation’ – highlighting a critical coordination gap. Operating from inaccessible forests along the Nigerien border, the group is able to launch attacks on civilians with relative impunity, underscoring the persistent issue of ungoverned spaces in Nigeria.
Hazard materialisation: A resurgence of the Lakurawa armed group has been confirmed in northwest Nigeria and across the Nigeria–Niger border. The group, which re-emerged in late 2024 amid weakened security coordination between Nigeria and Niger, has carried out multiple attacks on border communities, set up bases in remote forested areas, and increased recruitment and taxation in affected areas.

Risk Title: A return to large‑scale conflict in Gaza stokes a further deterioration of food security and humanitarian conditions
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
On 10 October 2025, Hamas and Israel agreed upon a new ceasefire following two previous ones. The first lasted between 24–30 November 2023 and the second from 19 January to 18 March 2024, and both proved to be fragile. Under the 2025 agreement, Israel and Hamas committed to a withdrawal and unimpeded humanitarian access; Israel began marking a ‘yellow line’ on 20 October 2025 as a withdrawal boundary.
This new ceasefire is also likely to collapse owing to several factors: repeated violations, Israeli control of at least 60% of the strip, continued restrictions on humanitarian access, a recent UNSC decision that ignores Palestinians’ right to self-govern, and escalations related to the US/Israel attacks on Iran.
According to the Gaza Government Media Office, between 10 October and 22 December 2025, Israel committed at least 875 separate violations of the ceasefire, killing 114 Palestinians and wounding 1,112 others. Repeated Israeli violations may eventually prompt a response from Hamas, contributing to a collapse of the ceasefire and a return to full-blown conflict.
Under the ceasefire, Israel was supposed to withdraw to the yellow line, but reports show that Israeli military positions remain established across Gaza, controlling roughly 58–60% of the territory, including key areas in Rafah, Khan Younis, and parts of Gaza city. Israeli forces have also repeatedly crossed beyond this yellow line, occupying more areas than the ceasefire intended for the long term. This de facto occupation undermines the possibility of a stable ceasefire, and Palestinians are likely to perceive it as annexation.
Israeli forces continue to control the flow of humanitarian aid, goods, fuel, building materials, and humanitarian shelters into Gaza. Despite the ceasefire, many aid convoys and shipments remain blocked, and key supplies, such as tents, medical equipment, generators, and construction materials, have been rejected or delayed. Humanitarian needs in Gaza continue to be very high, especially during winter (typically from November–March). For example, Storm Byron resulted in widespread flooding in Gaza on 11 December, affecting 55,000 families. Without unimpeded access to aid, basic survival needs cannot be met, increasing hardships among the population and raising the incentive for armed groups to resume fighting.
On 17 November 2025, the UNSC adopted a resolution backing a US-proposed stabilisation plan for Gaza, including the deployment of an “international stabilisation force” and transitional governance structures. Many Palestinians reject the resolution, arguing that it disregards their right to self-determination and places Gaza under de facto foreign control. They view it as undermining legitimate Palestinian governance, making the renewal of armed resistance more likely if the stabilisation force appears as foreign occupation rather than protection.
If a war erupts between Israel and Iran, it will likely prompt Israel to close all border crossings into Gaza and potentially intensify air strikes. This will highly contribute to a return to conflict in Gaza and a collapse of the ceasefire.
A renewed war will likely begin with intense Israeli aerial bombardment across all areas west of the yellow line, targeting what Israel identifies as Hamas positions but inevitably hitting densely populated neighbourhoods where civilians are sheltering in damaged buildings or makeshift tents. Ground incursions may follow, especially in the central and southern areas, where Israeli forces already maintain forward positions. Urban fighting would expand again into Deir Al Balah, Khan Younis, and the remaining parts of Gaza city. It is also likely that Palestinian militias backed by Israel will be deployed to launch attacks on Hamas and loot humanitarian convoys. Inside Gaza, armed groups, mainly Hamas, would resume rocket fire and improvised attacks from the remaining pockets where they operate. This would prompt further Israeli strikes and expand the combat zone.
