Risk Title: Permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line before the Israeli elections increases displacement and humanitarian access constraints
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
There is a high probability that Israeli forces will formally declare and physically enclose a permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line in the period leading up to Israel's October 2026 parliamentary elections, progressively reducing the territory accessible to civilians and humanitarian responders.
Since the 10 October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli forces have steadily expanded their military footprint beyond the initial demarcation line through tank advances, repeated evacuation orders, the construction of defensive positions, and localised operations. The Israeli-controlled area had expanded from 53% of Gaza Strip at the ceasefire to 64.9% by June 2026, with the trend notably intensifying late into the month. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data reports that events reflecting Yellow Line expansion and associated military movements increased from an average of fewer than four events per month between October 2025 and mid-June 2026 to 22 events between 18 June and 17 July 2026, a more than fivefold increase.

During the same period, activity by the Shuja’iyya Popular Defense Forces led by Rami Hilles, an anti-Hamas Palestinian armed group operating with Israeli support, also increased. Between 30 June and 9 July, the group carried out three recorded incidents targeting IDP camps in Gaza city's At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya neighbourhoods, including reported abductions and raids, indicating increasingly complex security dynamics around the expanding Yellow Line.

The period preceding Israel's October 2026 elections has a high probability of reinforcing this trajectory rather than prompting a fundamental shift in military strategy. The E1 settlement plan is a longstanding Israeli initiative that was revived in July 2025 after four years of suspension and approved for advancement by the Israeli Government on 20 August 2025. The plan aims to expand Ma’ale Adumim municipality and create a continuous built-up area between the Israeli settlements and Jerusalem city. Its implementation could further fragment the West Bank, particularly by disrupting geographic contiguity between central and southern areas, and increase the likelihood of severing East Jerusalem from the rest of the occupied West Bank. Its advancement could accelerate the displacement of entire Bedouin communities in the area, generating additional humanitarian needs.
Implementation has accelerated in 2026. In August, Israel issued a tender for 1,234 housing units in E1, followed on 17 September by a further 2,167 units, bringing the total to 3,401. Bidding on the 2,167-unit tender was scheduled to open on 25 October, two days before Israel's 27 October parliamentary elections.
Government efforts to advance the tenders before the election could accelerate implementation of the approved plan and trigger a faster-paced displacement. The awarding of tenders would allow the Israeli Government to move faster towards infrastructure works and construction, making the project more difficult for a future government to reverse. Implementation could accelerate if the tender process proceeds despite the postponement and the current Government retains power after the election. Current vulnerability / Coping capacitie:
The West Bank has high and worsening humanitarian needs, with 1.52 million people projected to need humanitarian assistance in 2026, compared with 1.2 million in 2025. Prolonged conflict, displacement, settler violence, settlement expansion, and movement restrictions have significantly eroded household coping capacity.
By September 2026, more than 1,600 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties or property damage had been recorded across the West Bank, affecting 275 Palestinian communities, nearly as many communities as during all of 2025 (279), while more than 4,000 Palestinians had been displaced since the start of the year by demolitions, evictions, settler attacks, and related access restrictions.
E1-affected communities face particularly limited coping capacity. The 18 Bedouin and herding communities living in the area of the planned E1 settlement, comprising about 4,000 people, have experienced sustained demolition and displacement pressure. Between 8–17 September, Israeli authorities demolished 32 structures in South ‘Anata and Tublas villages, displacing 66 Palestinians; both communities are near the area designated for E1 expansion. Access to land, water, and livelihoods is also constrained, mostly because of settler attacks. For example, in July 2026, settler activity damaged water infrastructure serving approximately 200 residents in Nkheila Bedouin community and restricted Palestinian access to grazing areas.
Bedouin communities in the E1/Ma’ale Adumim area rely heavily on grazing and livestock, while restrictions on land and grazing access directly undermine household livelihoods. A 2024 survey of 23 Bedouin communities across the West Bank found that 72% of respondents raise livestock and 59% had been attacked by settlers while grazing. No figure is available for the E1 communities alone.([OCHA 16/12/2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/flash-appeal-occupied-palestinian-territory-2026), [OCHA 12/09/2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-11-september-2026), [OCHA 25/05/2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-may-2026), [OCHA 25/07/2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-23-july-2026), [OCHA 28/09/2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-september-2026), [Doha Institute 15/03/2026](https://www.dohainstitute.org/ar/ResearchAndStudies/Pages/pastoral-settlement-policies-to-combat-the-latest-models-of-settlement-and-economic-exploitation.aspx)).

Risk Title: Continued protests across Panama, following the government's approval to exploit a mining area in a biodiverse jungle, result in access constraints and disruption of services and economic activities for some population groups
Rationale:
---------BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE-------
The Panamanian government signed a concession contract (arrangement between a public authority and an economic operator) with the Canadian mining company First Quantum Minerals, which allowed the latter to continue operating an open-pit copper mine in a richly biodiverse jungle. Panama’s National Assembly, the country’s legislative body, and the country’s president fast-tracked the contract and approved it on 20 October 2023. 

Since the contract was approved, Panama has been facing protests across the country. Protestors claim the contract was fast-tracked with little public input and lacks transparency, making allegations of corruption of the lawmakers. The protests are being led by construction workers, educators, indigenous groups, and activists, mainly calling for the revocation of the mining contract. Tens of thousands of people have been reported to be participating in the protests across the country. According to the protesters, there are significant environmental risks of the contract, including for the vital water sources required for water consumption.

As at 10 November 2023, the protests have generally been peaceful; ACLED data shows that around 80% of the protests occurring since 20 October 2023 have been peaceful and 20% violent demonstrations which include incidents of clashes between protestors and security forces, use of tear gas to disperse protestors, arrests, vandalism, and robbery. Significant increase in the deployment of security forces has been observed since the protests began. As at 14 November 2023, two fatalities have been reported: an elderly man was apparently frustrated with the blockage and tried to force the protestors to remove a barrier blocking the Pan American highway and then he allegedly opened fire on the protestors, killing two of them.

On 3 November 2023, the National Assembly signed an indefinite moratorium on new mining concessions into law, which also prohibits renewing existing concessions. However, the new law still allows Minera Panama, the Panamanian subsidiary of First Quantum Minerals, to operate. Hence, the protests are still ongoing. The country’s Supreme Court stated that it will consider two lawsuits filed against the renewed contract with First Quantum.

The protests led to countrywide road blockades that have negatively impacted the economy, transportation, food security, education, healthcare, and WASH, and raised protection concerns.
Due to the insecurity caused by the protests, educational authorities closed all schools across the country. 

There have been reports of attack on healthcare, including assault on healthcare personnel, ambulances, and vehicles transporting patients by people among the protestors. On 27 October 2023, the Panamanian National Operations Center requested interinstitutional support to the Red Cross Society of Panama to provide assistance, especially through healthcare services, to the population affected by the protests and blockades. The IFRC has initiated an operation targeting 3,500 people. In several provinces, supplies required for water purification are running low, leading to the risk of clean water rationing. 

Several areas in the provinces of Bocas del Toro, Chiriqui, Darien, Herrera, and Los Santos have reported fuel shortages and rationing of food supplies by supermarkets and stores. An electricity generation company, whose production depends on fossil fuels, has issued warnings of potential controlled power outages to manage the electricity supply.

Rice is the staple food in Panama. Darien, Herrera, Los Santos, and Chiriqui provinces comprise the primary rice producers. Rice mills are unable to distribute their stored rice during the harvest period due to road closures, resulting in considerable losses. Significant loss in perishable goods, including fruits and vegetables, have also been reported due to the inability to sell and transport perishable products to markets and storage facilities.

In early October of 2023, Panama and Costa Rica announced a plan to provide a bus service to quickly move thousands of migrants crossing the Darien Gap through Panama to the Costa Rican border. On 24 October, it was reported that more than 30 buses from Darien to Costa Rica were stranded in the Chiriqui as they could not move forward towards Costa Rica. On 25 October, another 20 buses were not permitted to pass in San Felix, Chiriqui province; as a result, the migrants on the buses started their journey by foot from San Felix to Paso Canoas, Costa Rica.

-----AGGRAVATING FACTORS--------
Copper is the major export good for Panama. Analysts estimate that revoking the mining contract would cut Panama’s GDP growth from a forecast 6% in 2023 to just 1%. So, repealing the mining contract will have significant negative impact on the economy; however, not repealing it would also likely cause significant negative environmental (and consequently economic) impacts. This situation is aggravated by the current drought, exacerbated by a severe El Nino weather system, which has reduced water levels in the Panama Canal, prompting the Panama Canal Authority to implement additional vessel reductions in an effort to conserve water.

--------EXPECTED IMPACT--------
Continued protests will worsen the abovementioned situation, which could lead to a political and socioeconomic crisis in Panama, and possibly to humanitarian consequences for some more exposed population groups, These consequences could include lack of healthcare support, education, and clean water in some areas of the countries. There would also be raising food insecurity concerns, loss of livelihoods, especially among rice and vegetable farmers, and heightening of protection concerns for those participating in protests that become violent. 

--------UPDATE--------
The risk has only partially materialised. The expected impact was not realised. So far, it has not generated humanitarian needs other than those already mentioned in the background and rationale section. 

Panama's Supreme Court of Justice ruled that Panama’s new mining contract with the Canadian company First Quantum was unconstitutional. Following the ruling, the president of the country said that a process to close the Cobre Panama mine was set to begin. Protests have also began to subside after the ruling.

The protests have already had significant impact on the economy. Retail associations estimated a loss of around US$200 million in the first 30 days of protests. Logistics losses are estimated to be around US$4.6 billion. 

Panama’s economy is heavily based on the ability to facilitate the transit of global merchandise, which has been negatively affected by the protests. The logistics sector has been estimated to account for around 20% of the country’s GDP and employs around 10% of the Panamanian workforce.

The protests also have reportedly reduced Panama’s attractiveness as a foreign investment destination. Large losses in the tourism and hospitality sectors have been reported, with many international tourists cancelling their trips to the country through January 2024. 

Shortages in food, fuel, and medicines have been reported in some cities and the government is importing such supplies from neighbouring Costa Rica to fill the gaps.

The company said that it has initiated international arbitration against Panama. Estimates suggest that Panama might have to pay at least US$20-50 billion (25-65% of the country’s GDP) if it loses the case. 

Livelihoods of the mine's employees and the people whose jobs are indirectly related to the mine are considered to be affected. The mine is reported to employ around 6,600 people (more than 5,500 are Panamanians). In total 40,000 jobs, directly and indirectly, are reportedly linked with the mine. 

It is to be noted that, if Panama loses the international arbitration case, which would be compounded by the negative impacts of the closure of the mine, there will likely be significant socio-economic distress in the country.

Risk Title: Deteriorating socioeconomic situation in Papua New Guinea trigger violent incidents such as riots in urban areas, heightening protection concerns
Rationale:
Papua New Guinea is marked by high youth unemployment and poverty, reduced purchasing power, lack of provision of basic services for its people, and poor governance. Only a quarter of the population who are engaged in work have formal, stable jobs. Many people reportedly flee from the violence-affected Highlands region to seek refuge and opportunities in urban centres, especially the capital of Papua New Guinea, Port Moresby. 
 
Nearly 60% of women and girls aged 15—49 have experienced some form of physical sexual violence, which is almost twice the global average. The overall state of the healthcare system is very poor, with lack of trained personnel, inadequate wages, a deteriorating infrastructure, and frequent lack of critical drugs and dressings.
 
Such underlying factors are considered to trigger social disruptions. In January 2024, the police went on strike over underpay, which was later revealed to be a technical glitch in the public servants’ payroll system. The initially peaceful protests turned into riots, comprising mass opportunistic looting, arson, and violence, mainly in Port Moresby. At least 15 people were killed in the riots, with some reports indicating a much higher number. Widespread sexual violence was also reported. 
 
Protests, riots, and incidents of violence against civilians in the non-Highlands areas rose significantly in 2023. The fragile social and economic situation may trigger more violence incidents, particularly riots, in non-Highlands urban centres in 2024. Lack of security forces’ capacity to deal violence also serves as an aggravating factor for riots.

UPDATE (05/01/2025)
The risk did not materialise. The fragile social and economic situation in Papua New Guinea has continued throughout 2024. However, no issues, such as government policies, triggered significant violent incidents, such as riots in urban areas. 

Riots stemming from tribal tensions and disputes have been common in the country and has continued in 2024. Riots and protests and fatalities related to such incidents in the entire country has fallen in 2024 compared to 2023.

Risk Title: Political violence and attacks by armed groups in Mindanao around the May presidential elections result in displacement and protection issues.
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
Electoral violence across the Philippines is a threat for the current three-month long election season that started on 8 February. Voters will choose the next president, vice president, and 18,000 other political positions on 9 May (The Diplomat 07/02/2022). Electoral violence by privately hired armed groups include voter intimidation, attacks on polls, and assassination of political rivals (Benar News 02/02/2022 ; New Mandala 08/07/2021 ; PNA 09/02/2022 ; University of Portsmouth 30/09/2021 and  08/10/2021 ; Rappler 14/02/2022; Inquirer 01/12/2021).    

The leading candidate is Ferdinand Marcos Jr., son of Ferdinand Marcos, who held the presidency from 1965 until he was ousted in a people’s revolution in 1986 (Aljazeera 14/12/2022 ; VOA 06/01/2022). In southern Mindanao, Marcos’ policies contributed to land grabs, human rights abuses, and conflict (Inquirer 28/12/2016; Asia Society 08/03/2022). The controversial Marcos Jr.’s candidacy will likely contribute to increased political tensions and violence in Mindanao.   

Mindanao is still affected by ongoing armed group attacks and their clashes with the military. Armed groups, including the New People’s Army (NPA), Maute, Abu Sayyaf, and Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters all refuse peace talks and negotiations with the government, and seek independence from the Philippines (Global Initiative 20/02/2020).  These armed groups may conduct more attacks than usual, taking advantage of the political tensions and authorities’ focus on the elections. Security forces are already being deployed to areas of security concerns across the country, most of which are in Mindanao (Business Mirror 14/02/2022).   

Intercommunal violence in the form of clan feuds including over land disputes also affects Mindanao and causes displacement. Conflict and violence in Mindanao are exacerbated by a shadow economy that provides economic and political means for the groups involved (Global Initiative 20/02/2020; International Alert 04/2014). Mindanao is therefore at a high risk of increased violence and armed groups attacks, including electoral violence by ‘private’ armed groups hired to attack polls and political candidates by rivaling politicians (Benar News 30/06/2021; PhilStar 15/02/2022; Philippine Army 13/01/2022). Polls situated in areas with armed groups presence, particularly the NPA, are most at risk (New Mandala 08/07/2021; Manila Bulletin 13/02/2022).
Hazard materialisation: In the months preceding the election in the month of May, especially in April, there was a rise in armed conflict in the Mindanao islands.

Risk Title: La Niña-driven above-normal rainfall and enhanced cyclonic activity in the Philippines cause widespread flooding, agricultural damage, and displacement
Rationale: La Niña arrived in the Philippines in October 2025 and is likely to persist until February–March 2026. La Niña events have typically been linked to a higher frequency of tropical cyclones late in the year, along with increased rainfall and flood risk across much of the country. Current seasonal forecasts anticipate a high probability of above-average precipitation and above-average temperatures between November 2025 and March 2026. This indicates that between late 2025 and early 2026, the country could face compounding hazards, including storms and intense northeast monsoon rains, which may cause widespread flooding and landslides, especially across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. Coastal and riverine communities in the Bicol region, Eastern Visayas, and Mindanao are particularly exposed, while informal urban settlements in Metro Manila and Cebu face a high risk of waterlogging and infrastructure collapse. Dam overflows and disrupted transport routes could isolate villages, delay aid delivery, and damage essential facilities, such as schools, health centres, and evacuation sites. The humanitarian consequences are expected to be severe: displacement, loss of livelihoods, and growing food insecurity among farming and fishing families. Waterborne and vector-borne diseases (such as leptospirosis, cholera, and dengue) may also surge because of stagnant floodwaters and poor sanitation. These risks will strain an already overburdened health system recovering from successive disasters. La Niña could push thousands of households into renewed crisis throughout the first half of 2026, amplifying humanitarian needs nationwide. Risk Title: El Niño-driven agricultural losses and water shortages in the Philippines increase food security, WASH, and health needs
Rationale:
The Philippines faces an increasing risk of El Niño-driven drought, potentially triggering water shortages, agricultural losses, and heat stress in the coming months. El Niño conditions are already present in the tropical Pacific, with sea surface temperature anomalies reaching the +0.5° C threshold in May 2026; most models indicate an over 80% probability of full development, persisting until early 2027 at strong to very strong intensity.
Seasonal forecasts anticipate below-average precipitation across central and southern regions from July–September, extending nationwide from October. The provinces likely to be affected are Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Kalinga, La Union, Mountain Province, Nueva Ecija, Nueva Vizcaya, Pangasinan, Quirino, and Tarlac. Temperatures are forecast above seasonal averages nationwide from July–December. This is likely to produce a poor monsoon season (May–October), vital for maize and rice production, affecting both rain-fed and irrigated crops. Main season rice, harvested in December, accounts for 60% of domestic production.
The Philippines has experienced 12 major drought events since 1968. It is estimated that agricultural drought caused approximately 20 million metric tons of crop losses between 1980–2020. Between July 2023 and April 2024, El Niño-related dry conditions affected multiple provinces, causing agricultural losses, water shortages, and livelihood disruptions. The Department of Social Welfare and Development reported thousands of farming households affected by prolonged dry spells, with losses in some provinces reaching hundreds of millions of pesos. This event also drove extreme heat, school disruptions, and mounting pressure on water and food systems – illustrating how El Niño can rapidly become a multisector humanitarian crisis for affected communities.
In the next one to three months, primary concerns include localised rainfall deficits, water stress, and heat-related impacts, particularly in affected agricultural zones. Over the next three to six months, if El Niño strengthens as projected, drought conditions could intensify significantly, leading to reduced crop yields, livestock stress, water shortages, rising food prices, and worsening livelihood pressures. This may increase humanitarian needs in the WASH, food security, and health sectors, particularly in already-vulnerable rural communities. ([PAGASA accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/climate/el-nino-la-nina/monitoring), [PIA 05/06/2026](https://pia.gov.ph/news/el-nino-to-emerge-in-june-intensify-into-strong-to-very-strong-condition-by-year-end-pagasa/), [FAO accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.fao.org/in-action/drought-portal/preparedness/vulnerability-and-impact-assessment/national-case-studies/the-philippines-case/en), [WB accessed 17/06/2026](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/country/philippines/enso), [GMA 26/04/2026](https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/weather/content/985366/drought-philippines-2026/story/))

Title: Below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures
Description: 
El Niño typically suppresses rainfall across the Philippines while also contributing to above-average temperatures. During the monsoon season, it also contributes to irregular rainfall distribution, characterized by intermittent dry spells and uneven precipitation.  Reduced or unheavenly distributed rainfall, combined with high temperatures, increases evapotranspiration, accelerating the depletion of soil moisture, while reduced precipitation affect surface and groundwater reserves. This can significantly reduce water availability for domestic consumption, irrigation, and livestock, particularly in drought-prone and agriculture-dependent provinces. Prolonged heat and moisture stress can also damage crops during critical growth stages, reduce agricultural productivity, and increase heat-related health risks, especially among affected rural households and outdoor workers.

Risk Title: Conflict in Mogadishu between pro-Government and pro-opposition military forces, as well as increased Al-Shabaab attacks, result in displacement and humanitarian access constraints
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
In Somalia, the failure to hold general elections by February 2021 created disagreements and high levels of tension between the Government and the opposition, which culminated in conflict in Mogadishu in April 2021. Parliamentary elections were set for October–November 2021, but most states did not conclude elections within that period. Resentment among the opposition rose as the President continued to stay in office long past his mandated term.

In September 2021, a rift between the President and Prime Minister raised political tensions, polarised the country, and nearly resulted in conflict. While this rift ended in a truce in October 2021, another political stalemate began in December 2021, with both the President and Prime Minister blaming each other for stalled elections. The international community made significant mediation efforts to de-escalate tensions. Any political stalemate in Mogadishu risks affecting the functioning of security institutions. Coupled with a lack of cohesion within the army, this could result in increased insecurity across the country, with armed groups potentially intensifying fighting and gaining more territorial control.
Al-Shabaab has already increased its attacks countrywide as part of an attempt to derail the electoral process. These attacks may continue to escalate as elections are repeatedly delayed, and factions of the army could clash again in Mogadishu.
Hazard materialisation: Political instability and a reduced focus on counterterrorism provided Al-Shabaab an opportunity to intensify attacks. Al-Shabaab launched more frequent assaults in 2021, targeting government officials, civilians, and infrastructure.

Risk Title: Escalating tensions around universal suffrage in Somalia heightens conflict and instability ahead of the 2026 elections
Rationale:
Somalia is transitioning from a clan-based indirect electoral system to universal suffrage for the 2026 elections, marking the first attempt in over 50 years to hold nationwide one-person-one-vote polls. In August 2025, the Federal Government and opposition leaders signed an agreement establishing the framework for parliament members to be directly elected. The agreement has also deepened rifts within the main opposition coalition, the Forum for National Salvation, with former president Sharif Sheikh Ahmed insisting that the prevailing insecurity makes the implementation of such extensive electoral reforms unfeasible.
While representing democratic progress, this shift is occurring in a fragile political environment marked by unresolved disputes between the Federal Government and federal member states (FMSes). Puntland has rejected the constitutional reforms underpinning universal suffrage, warning of potential violence. Jubaland state has also experienced armed clashes over disputed electoral processes in recent years.
As voter registration rolls out and constituency boundaries are drawn, clan grievances and FMS–Federal Government tensions are likely to intensify. This political disunity, characterised by persistent rivalries and potential boycotts from opposition and states such as Puntland and Jubaland, will impede unified counterterrorism efforts, consequently increasing overall insecurity and humanitarian needs. Regions and dominant clans feeling marginalised may resist the reforms politically or militarily, sparking localised violence as they seek to assert control. If the elections are ultimately delayed, boycotted, or politically contested, the resulting legitimacy crisis could also escalate into violent clashes or a governance breakdown. Specifically, the collapse of the federal electoral process risks reigniting widespread clan conflicts and political violence.
Simultaneously, Al Shabaab is poised to exploit this instability. Leveraging an intensification of offensives and territorial gains expected in 2025, the group will target voter registration sites, polling centres, and civilians. Risk Title: Consecutive below-average rains amid expected La Niña conditions in northern and central Somalia deepen drought Impacts
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
A below-average Deyr season (October–December), the third consecutive poor rainy season in northern and central areas, is forecast, at the same time that the probability of La Niña conditions is projected to reach around 60%. This climatic development is expected to reduce rainfall across much of Somalia, prolonging dry conditions and intensifying the effects of several consecutive below-average rainfall seasons. River levels in the Shabelle and Juba River Basins are likely to drop further, increasing water scarcity in riverine and agropastoral zones. Reduced rainfall coupled with rising temperatures will accelerate crop and livestock losses, placing rural livelihoods under severe strain.
In key food-producing regions, such as Bakool, Bay, and Lower Shabelle, maize and groundnut yields have already declined by up to 40% during previous drought years. Many of these areas have shifted from being net exporters to net consumers of basic staples. Declining soil fertility and shrinking pasture resources are expected to raise livestock mortality rates significantly, particularly in Galgaduud, Gedo, and Togdheer. This will erode household incomes and undermine a critical source of national exports.
The deterioration of water infrastructure is a pressing concern. Extended dry periods have reduced groundwater recharge and increased salinity, especially in coastal and riverine areas, making many sources unsafe for consumption and raising health risks. Access to safe water and functional health services continues to diminish, with approximately 40 primary healthcare facilities and 16 mobile health teams closing across 21 districts. Water contamination and displacement have contributed to favourable conditions for disease outbreaks, with more than 6,550 cases of cholera and acute watery diarrhoea reported between January–July.
The compounded impacts of failed rains, collapsing rural livelihoods, and disruptions to basic services are expected to heighten food insecurity and trigger further displacement, particularly in Bakool, Bay, Galgaduud, Gedo, and parts of Mudug and Lower Shabelle. Resource scarcity will likely fuel localised tensions and competition over water and grazing areas, especially between pastoralist and farming communities as well as among ethnic clans. Armed group activity is also expected to intensify, with Al Shabaab likely exploiting the drought to strengthen territorial control. Tactics may include imposing informal taxes on herders and traders, restricting access to water points and interfering with humanitarian aid delivery to consolidate influence. ([OCHA 21/09/2025] (https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/somalia/somalia-monthly-humanitarian-update-august-2025), [OCHA 05/08/2025] (https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/somalia/somalia-drought-conditions-central-and-northern-regions-flash-update-no1-5-august-2025) [ICPAC 26/08/2025] (https://www.icpac.net/news/below-normal-rains-and-warmer-than-usual-conditions-are-expected-over-most-parts-of-the-greater-horn-of-africa/))
Hazard materialisation: The climate hazard partially materialised, although not through the initially anticipated La Niña mechanism. Instead of La Niña-driven below-average Deyr rainfall, Somalia experienced a continuation of drought conditions following failed 2025 Deyr rains and an unusually harsh Jilaal season. By early 2026, drought conditions had intensified, with forecasts indicating delayed and uneven recovery during the 2026 Gu season. The shift towards El Niño later in 2026 changed the expected hazard profile from prolonged drought to a potential drought-to-flood transition, particularly in the Juba and Shabelle River Basins.

Risk Title: The escalation of political and armed conflict in Southwest state leads to large‑scale displacement and worsens humanitarian conditions
Rationale:
Rising tensions between Southwest state authorities and the Federal Government of Somalia continue to significantly increase the probability of armed confrontation and large‑scale displacement in the coming weeks and months. The formal severing of ties with Mogadishu, federal declarations that the Southwest leadership’s mandate has expired, and mutual accusations over the diversion of weapons and security interference point to a deepening political rift. Around Baidoa, deployment orders for regional forces and reported movements of federal troops indicate an elevated risk of localised clashes escalating into a wider confrontation, particularly if no negotiated settlement is reached before key political milestones. Upcoming electoral processes in Southwest state and nationwide are likely to further heighten tensions, as competition over power and representation may trigger protests, the contestation of results, or targeted violence around Baidoa and other strategic locations.
At the same time, Southwest state faces severe and compounding humanitarian pressures that would heighten the impact of any political or security escalation. Prolonged drought has already driven mass internal displacement from districts such as Waajid and other parts of Bay and Bakool, eroding pastoral and agropastoral livelihoods and sharply increasing food insecurity. Many displaced families have moved towards Baidoa and other already-overstretched host areas, where services, water availability, and livelihood opportunities are extremely limited. Further conflict‑related displacement from urban centres or along key road corridors would add to existing caseloads, strain coping capacity, and heighten protection risks, including family separation, exploitation, and gender‑based violence. Risk Title: Escalating violence between the Sudan People's Liberation Movement and the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-in-Opposition reignites civil war, driving mass displacement and service collapse
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
The collapse of the 2018 revitalized peace agreement and the disbandment of the unity government have dramatically increased the risk of South Sudan sliding back into full-scale civil conflict. The March 2025 arrest of First Vice President Riek Machar of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition by President Salva Kiir has reignited ethnically charged fighting between Dinka and Nuer armed forces, with clashes already concentrated in Jonglei and Upper Nile states. Up to 300,000 newly displaced people add to the approximately two million already internally displaced and over ten million – two-thirds of the population – requiring some form of humanitarian assistance, including 7.5 million projected to face food insecurity during the April–July lean season. South Sudan has suffered from chronic violence since independence. The collapse of the peace framework ahead of elections, accompanied by the re-emergence of organised, ethnically mobilised armed groups, represents the risk of a return to full-scale civil war.
Several factors increase the likelihood of deterioration into civil war. The taking and retaking of Akobo signals an escalation beyond the fragmented, subnational violence that characterised the 2018–2024 period, with organised armed groups now contesting territory at a scale not seen since the first civil war. The mobilisation of Nuer armed groups, including the White Army, suggests this is a coordinated insurgency with the capacity to sustain prolonged fighting. Uganda's continued deployment of troops in support of Kiir's Government risks drawing the conflict into a broader regional confrontation, and spillover from Sudan and Ethiopia could further destabilise border areas. Over 1.36 million people have already arrived in South Sudan from Sudan since April 2023, with services in border areas stretched to breaking point; an additional 380,000 arrivals are projected by the end of 2026. The planned December 2026 elections, already twice postponed, will intensify political competition and may become a flashpoint for renewed violence, whether they proceed or are cancelled again. The risk has intensified after President Kiir dissolved the transitional government on 22 September, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December. It followed amendments to the National Elections Act, signed on 21 September, that allow Kiir to remain in office with full powers throughout the election period. Kiir had also dismissed the chair of the National Elections Commission on 15 September without giving a reason. The South Sudan Opposition Movements Alliance has rejected the caretaker administration as illegitimate and the elections as a sham, and warned on 28 September that the crisis could lead to further violence and insecurity across the country. The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, which had already warned in August that elections without safeguards and inclusive dialogue could fuel renewed conflict and atrocity crimes, said the window to prevent a return to 2013–2018 levels of violence and displacement is closing. Government and Sudan People's Liberation Army-in-Opposition forces continue to fight in Jonglei and Upper Nile states, a conflict that predates the election, and no escalation directly linked to the election has been reported so far. By advancing in Blue Nile state, RSF seeks to strengthen its position to recapture and control central Sudan, later opening a route through Sennar state. 
Following heavy territorial losses in 2025, including entire states in central Sudan, RSF has reconstituted its operational capacity through its alliance with Abdelaziz Adam al Hilu's Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N/Al Hilu). Access to terrain under its control has provided RSF with defensive depth, cross-border supply lines, and logistical continuity. This enables it to sustain multifront operations and power its advance in Blue Nile, positioning the RSF for a prolonged and expanded offensive rather than a short-term tactical push and increasing the likelihood of escalation beyond the current front lines.

Risk Title: Long-range RSF drones targeting the eastern supply corridor and Port Sudan disrupt trade and aid delivery in Red Sea state
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale: RSF tactics have increasingly shifted from ground offensives in SAF-controlled areas to long-range drone strikes. The May 2025 strikes on Port Sudan's fuel reservoirs demonstrated RSF's capacity to hit locations far from its main areas of control using long-range kamikaze drones. Port Sudan remains a strategic target because it continues to host key government, technical, and logistical functions, while the Port Sudan-Kassala-Gedaref corridor remains central to Sudan's economy and humanitarian response. Before the conflict, this corridor handled most international trade, and it continues to support imports, fuel supplies, and humanitarian cargo entering SAF-controlled areas. Targeting the corridor would allow RSF to undermine SAF supply chains and disrupt commercial and aid flows without needing to control territory in eastern Sudan. Risk Title: Türkiye's military incursion into northern Syria triggered by the nearing general elections results in the displacement of people from areas of conflict.
Rationale:
In May 2022, Türkiye announced that it plans to continue its 30km military incursion into northern Syria, along the border, as part of its regional conflict against Kurdish armed groups that considers part of PKK network. Türkiye also announced plans to move 1 million Syrians back to Syria. This is a renewed rhetoric from similar statements in October 2021.

On 1 June, President Erdogan confirmed some of the areas that will be targeted sometime in the future when the military operation takes place: Tal Rifat and Manbij cities. He added that once these cities are under control, the forces will move to other areas, which means Kobani and the areas north of M4 route are likely to be targeted in the military offensive. Türkiye would seek to link the two separated areas under its control in northeast Syria.

Displacement and protection concerns are likely for the civilians living in the area. The estimated population of Tal Rifaat, Manbij (450,000), and Kobani is over 500,000.

The probability of an offensive was still low in June, with no significant military deployment at the border. The Turkish military plan has been opposed by the US, Russia and Iran., the Syrian government, and the de facto Kurdish authorities in the north, and is only backed by the Syrian armed groups that Turkey supports. 

In August, Turkiye announced that it is in the last stage of preparations for the military incursion into northern Syria. In the same month, the Turkish president hinted at readiness to contact the Syrian government. By late September, it became known that the Turkish intelligence chief held multiple meetings with the Syrian counterpart in Damascus, likely because of Russian mediation. 

In November an explosion hit the center of Istanbul, killing six and wounded 81 people. Turkish authority blamed the PKK/YPG in Northwest Syria for the explosion and is said the commands for the attack came from Kobane city, a Kurdish stronghold in Northwest Syria.

In the event of an incursion, there is also a low yet existing possibility of ISIS taking advantage of the conflict escalation to increase attacks across northern Syria, with the SDF being focused on fighting against the Turkish military.

Inflation rate has reached over 80% in October 2022, the highest in 24 years. High inflation and the economic crisis is the main challenge for the ruling party in next year's election. In early October, Erdogan renewed his pledge to send one million Syrians back to Syria at the Parliament. As the economic crisis deteriorates and opposition parties in Turkiye regularly call for Syrians to return to Syria, the issue is increasingly likely to shape the upcoming election season.
Current vulnerability / Coping capacitie: Kurds, and other minorities who are at risk of abuse by Turkish-backed armed groups. Women, children, elderly are most vulnerable in times of conflict and displacement

Risk Title: Escalations between loyalists to former President Bashar Al Assad and Sunni armed groups result in internal and cross-border displacement
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
There is a high risk of tensions escalating between groups still loyal to the former President and others affiliated with the transitional Government. Resulting clashes in the next months could affect communities along religious lines, particularly conflict between Alawite communities and Sunni groups. The formation of armed groups, such as the Military Council to Liberate Syria, localised in western Syria and led by former Al Assad army commanders, indicates the likelihood of organised resistance against the transitional Government. Conflict dynamics are likely to be localised but could evolve into sectarian clashes in mixed-population areas, such as Homs and parts of Rural Damascus. Road blockages, targeted assassinations, and raids on civilian populations are likely scenarios, considering what already transpired in March 2025: clashes began on 6 March after armed Al Assad loyalists ambushed a security force convoy near Lattakia, killing 13 officers and prompting a harsh military response from the transitional Government’s allied forces. Between 6–8 March, transitional Government security operations targeting Alawite neighbourhoods and villages in Hama, Lattakia, and Tartous killed at least 396 people, predominantly Alawite civilians. Unconfirmed estimates indicate up to 1,500 fatalities during these attacks.
The current sociopolitical dynamics in the country point towards a high probability of an escalation of social tensions along sectarian lines. The dismantling of Al Assad’s security apparatus without a clear reintegration plan, such as restoring former personnel to comparable roles or maintaining their salaries, has deepened a sense of marginalisation among many former President Al Assad loyalists, most of whom are Alawite. Attempts by the new authorities to absorb some of these forces into the new national army have largely been met with suspicion, both from opposition groups — those who previously opposed Al Assad’s regime — and other minority communities, such as Druze and Kurds. These minority communities are concerned about the potential return of oppressive practices, referring both to the military tactics that the Al Assad regime used and to fears that former regime loyalists could regain influence. The latter has the potential to drive imbalances in representation within the new forces, as Kurdish and Druze participation remains limited or symbolic in key command structures.
Minority groups, including the Alawite community, are also concerned that the War Spoils Committee, originally established in 2015 in Idleb to confiscate the properties of Al Assad loyalists, may resume its activities in Damascus and other parts of Syria under the new transitional Government, despite reports that its operations have been dormant and rebranded in 2022 under different names, such as the Properties Committee or Housing Institution. The confiscation of properties will further economically marginalise the Alawite and aggravate tensions. Some reports indicate that confiscations have resumed, though there has been no official announcement that the War Spoils Committee has been re-established. In January 2025, unidentified armed men claiming to be from the General Security Service of the transitional Government ordered an unknown number of Alawite families to evict their homes in Damascus.
Despite the factors contributing to the likelihood of further clashes between Al Assad loyalists and Sunni armed groups, there are efforts aimed at de-escalation. President Ahmed Al Sharaa has condemned the killings of Alawites and pledged to hold all involved accountable, including those within his own ranks. In March, he announced the formation of an independent national committee comprising judges to specifically investigate the events and violations in coastal areas. The committee has also engaged in controversial dialogue with figures from the Al Assad Government, including Fadi Saqr, a former commander of the National Defence Forces accused of abuses against Sunni civilians, as part of broader efforts to engage Alawite communities and prevent renewed violence.
If the investigations are delayed or neglected and the grievances among Alawite communities are not adequately addressed, particularly demands for justice, transparent accountability for the killings, and protection from further reprisal, besides addressing fears of exclusion and collective punishment, this will likely contribute to further violence. Already, the Alawite have found unwelcome a three-month extension beginning in April granted by President Al Sharaa on the deadline for the investigation of the coastal killings, stating concerns of buying time to hide facts. ([ACAPS 22/07/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

Current vulnerability / Coping capacitie: The overall humanitarian situation remains dire, with 16.5 million people projected to need humanitarian assistance across all sectors in 2025. More IDPs and refugees are returning to their hometowns since 8 December 2024, and they need resettlement and employment assistance. By 26 June 2025, more than 1.5 million IDPs and 628,000 refugees had returned to their places of origin. Many return to damaged or unaffordable shelters with poor infrastructure and shortages of critical services, including water, healthcare, electricity, and food. They also struggle with unsafe conditions, such as unexploded ordnance (UXO), crime, a lack of jobs, exploitative wages, and high transportation costs, all of which make rebuilding their lives extremely difficult, especially for women-headed households and those with children. The presence of landmines and UXO continues to be a key issue that restricts people’s movement and endangers their lives. Since December 2024, about 1,000 people, including many children, had died from mines and other remnants of war by June 2025. Expected impact:
If violence between Al Assad loyalists and the transitional Government intensifies, humanitarian needs are likely to increase, particularly in Alawite-majority areas. New waves of displacement may occur from Lattakia, Tartous, and parts of Homs – areas already hosting affected populations from earlier stages of the Syrian conflict. The March clashes displaced at least 51,000 people, who have fled the coastal regions to safer areas, including Homs and parts of Damascus governorates.
Clashes are more likely to occur in coastal regions, resulting in displacement from these areas. Should tensions increase in mixed areas such as Damascus, Homs, and surrounding inland areas, however, many Alawites may decide to move to coastal areas, viewing them as a safer stronghold given their Alawite-majority population and existing family properties originally intended for holiday or future contingency.
The humanitarian impact could again extend beyond Syria’s borders. Lebanon, already hosting more than 1.5 million Syrian refugees, could experience additional refugee flows, especially to Akkar governorate in northern Lebanon given its geographical proximity. Until 2 May, more than 36,700 people arrived from Syria to northern Lebanon as they fled the clashes between Al Assad loyalists and Sunni armed groups in March. The new arrivals are not registered as refugees, since UNHCR suspended registration in May 2015 per Lebanese Government decisions, restricting their movement and access to services. Relatives generally host these refugees from Syria, most of whom hope to seek asylum abroad, primarily in Europe. If arrivals from western Syria to northern Lebanon increase, the already limited access to services, such as shelter, water, electricity, and education, will likely be strained further. This may lead to tensions with host communities and Sunni Syrian refugees already residing in Lebanon given historical sectarian divisions and the perception that Alawites are aligned with Al Assad’s rule. Alawites are unlikely to displace to Jordan because western Syria, where most Alawites reside, does not share a direct border with the country, making access difficult. In one January raid, 25 people were arrested, of whom 17 were subsequently released. By 26 January, the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights had documented 18 deaths in retaliatory killings in 2026, including 11 in Homs governorate. Risk Title: The escalation of clashes between Druze and Sunni armed groups leads to displacement and increased needs for food, shelter, water, and healthcare
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
A further escalation of clashes between Sunni armed groups and Druze communities is likely, following a sectarian flare-up in late April 2025 and the transitional Government’s failure to contain the security fallout. Escalations may spread across Al Sweida and southern Damascus districts, particularly if Israel’s involvement intensifies or Druze factions become fragmented further.
On 26 April, a fabricated audio recording attributed to a Druze individual insulting the Prophet Muhammad circulated online, prompting enraged Sunni non-state armed groups to attack Druze neighbourhoods near Damascus. Clashes broke out on 28 April in the predominantly Druze districts of Jaramana and Sahnaya in Damascus as local Druze fighters exchanged fire with Sunni gunmen. The fighting spread south to Al Sweida governorate in villages including Al Soura Al Kubra, Ira, and Rasas, killing around 100 people from both sides. The clashes displaced an unknown number of families from some affected areas, likely within the governorate and temporarily.
The transitional Government’s inability to maintain security, coupled with weak control over Sunni armed groups, has emerged as a major trigger for renewed Druze-Sunni clashes. Some of these militias have independently targeted minority communities, including the Druze. Sunni armed groups, whether affiliated with the transitional Government or operating independently, are likely to launch further attacks on Druze-populated areas in Al Sweida and around Damascus, especially along the Damascus–Al Sweida highway and the Al Sweida–Dar’a border.
Sunni armed groups in Syria may target Druze communities for a combination of sectarian and strategic reasons. Some Sunni factions, including former HTS members, have historically viewed the Druze as heretical, leading to attacks, forced conversions, and property seizures justified by extremist ideology. Al Sweida is also important for Sunni armed groups to control because of its strategic location and political symbolism. Geographically, it borders key Sunni-dominated regions such as Dar’a and provides access to smuggling routes into Jordan, making it a vital corridor for the movement of fighters, weapons, and supplies. Politically, asserting control over Al Sweida allows Sunni factions to disrupt any future attempts at Druze autonomy or external support from Druze populations in Lebanon and the Golan Heights.
In response, Druze fighters are expected to retaliate, particularly in the absence of swift and effective intervention by the authorities. Previous government efforts to contain the violence have failed, as affiliated militias have themselves been involved in the clashes, exposing deep operational fragmentation. In April, the Government deployed limited forces and attempted mediation, but divisions within the security apparatus and perceived bias towards Sunni factions weakened its response. This fractured security landscape has intensified mistrust among Druze communities, especially following the mass killings of Alawites by Sunni armed groups in March 2025, an outcome the Druze fear they may also face. As a result, Druze militias have refused to disarm, with no indication that the transitional Government can address its current issue of having weak state control.
Israel will likely deepen its involvement, shifting from air strikes to deploying troops or proxies near the Druze-majority areas under the pretext of protecting them, risking confrontation with the transitional Government. In such cases, fighting could erupt in Al Sweida and surrounding villages, the outskirts of Damascus (Jaramana and Sahnaya), and possibly Quneitra, where the Druze are mostly located. Displacement from Druze-majority and nearby Sunni areas will likely follow, increasing humanitarian needs.
Israel’s interference in the tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government is likely to drive wider confrontations between Druze and Sunni armed groups, especially in the case of further Israeli ground incursions or the direct arming of Druze factions. In the clashes that happened in late April, Israeli drones and jets targeted Sunni armed groups near Sahnaya and bombed sites close to the presidential palace in Damascus. While Israel claimed these were defensive actions in support of the Druze, most Druze leaders have rejected the gesture, fearing it serves Israeli interests in expansion and not theirs. It also portrays them as allies to Israel, an idea that most Druze reject. Syrian officials have condemned the strikes as violations of sovereignty, and activists have accused Israel of using the clashes between the Druze and Sunni armed groups to justify deeper interference and military expansion in southern Syria.
A compounding factor likely to aggravate this conflict and the subsequent humanitarian impact is growing division among the Druze. Some Druze groups, including leaders from the Men of Dignity movement, have engaged with the transitional Government, joined ceasefire talks between Druze and Sunni armed groups, and integrated into local security forces to protect their areas. Others, led by figures such as Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, have rejected cooperation, calling the Government ‘terrorists’ and demanding international protection. Some activists in Al Sweida have even called for Druze self-governance over Al Sweida, citing instances in the past when the Druze managed their own affairs independently. So far, no fighting has broken out internally between Druze factions, but tensions are rising. If one side accuses the other of compromising community safety, local clashes are likely to erupt, causing more insecurity in affected areas in southern Syria or some districts in Damascus. Fractures among the Druze community can also allow for foreign interference from Israel or create openings for Sunni armed groups to attack the Druze again, possibly leading to further tensions.
De-escalation between Druze and Sunni armed groups depends on the transitional Government’s ability to control Sunni militias and protect Druze areas. Local ceasefires show that dialogue with Druze leaders can lead to a de-escalation of fighting, avoiding further clashes. That said, these arrangements remain fragile given some opposing Druze factions rejecting deals, local resistance to disarmament, the absence of official investigations into the violence, and the role of external parties such as Israel, whose interventions can contribute to deepening sectarian divisions. ([ACAPS 22/07/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

If clashes erupt in Al Sweida, it will likely push many Druze households to flee, mostly towards Dar’a and Rural Damascus. Some Druze may attempt to cross into northern Jordan given its geographical proximity to the conflict-affected areas in southern Syria. The displaced will likely seek to reach Al Azraq governorate in Jordan, as it hosts the majority of the Druze community in the country. Most of Syria’s Druze are likely to remain internally displaced within the country given their strong communal and territorial ties. In 2025, Syria already hosts 7.4 million IDPs, including 627,000 in Rural Damascus, 84,600 in Dar’a, and 53,000 in Al Sweida, while Jordan hosts 654,000 Syrian refugees.
If clashes in Druze-majority areas escalate, displaced families will likely urgently need food, shelter, water, and healthcare. With 14.5 million people already food-insecure across Syria, including over 221,000 in Al Sweida, further disruptions will worsen food access. Displacement could force people into unfinished or abandoned buildings without basic supplies. Damaged water systems may increase reliance on unsafe sources, raising disease risk. Risk Title: Further Israeli expansion in southern Syria triggers armed group resistance, displacement, and heightened food insecurity
Rationale:
Israel is likely to expand deeper into southern Syria to prevent a potential return of Iran-backed militias, such as Hezbollah, and respond to escalating sectarian violence, particularly near Druze communities, under the pretext of security and humanitarian intervention. This expansion, driven by the transitional Government’s inability to maintain control and provide protection, could result in further displacement and local clashes.
Immediately after the fall of Al Assad’s rule in December 2024, Israel expanded its presence in southern Syria, seizing the demilitarised buffer zone (around 400km²) beyond the Golan Heights and occupying strategic areas in Quneitra, including Tel Al Hara and several border villages. The Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) launched intensive air strikes targeting Syrian and Iranian military infrastructure, significantly weakening local resistance, which included remnants of Syrian army units and Iran-backed militias still active in the area at the time. These moves prompted clashes and displacement, notably from villages such as Al Hameidiyyeh, Rasem Al Rawadi, and Um Batna in Quneitra, with at least 100 Syrian families forcibly displaced by December. Many displaced civilians fled to Damascus or safer towns outside Israeli-held territory.
Israel sees the potential return of Iran-backed militias, especially Hezbollah, as a driver for further expansion in southern Syria, regardless of how likely that return may be. Although many of these forces withdrew after Al Assad’s fall, Israeli officials remain concerned they will regroup in areas near the Golan Heights, such as Quneitra and parts of western Dar’a governorate. The IDF are already positioned just over 20km from Damascus and have declared the presence of any Iranian or Iranian-backed groups a red line, indicating it would trigger immediate air strikes or other military responses to prevent their advancement near Israeli-controlled areas. The transitional Government has condemned the Israeli presence but avoided direct confrontation, focusing instead on internal stability. If Hezbollah attempts to re-establish rocket sites or weapon routes, Israel will likely push deeper into Quneitra or even Dar’a to enforce its buffer zone.
If sectarian attacks escalate near Israeli-held areas, especially against Druze communities, Israel is also likely to expand its presence in Syria under the pretext of protecting the minorities. For example, in April 2025, the IDF conducted air strikes near Damascus, targeting Sunni armed groups accused of attacking Druze civilians in Sahnaya district in the governorate, and subsequently evacuated three wounded Druze individuals to Israeli hospitals. Israel has publicly committed to protecting Syrian Druze. With Sunni and other armed groups subjecting Druze-majority towns to attacks, any assault may prompt a group of Druze leaders to seek Israeli help, especially the ones following Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, who is trying to establish stronger relations with Israel. A wider Israeli incursion into Al Sweida may be framed as a humanitarian intervention to protect Druze civilians from sectarian violence or Government-affiliated militias, though most Druze still reject annexation and prefer local autonomy within Syria under the transitional Government.
Another factor triggering Israel’s expansion into southern Syria is the transitional Government’s continued struggle with lack of security. Some non-state armed groups remain active in Quneitra and Dar’a. With some of Al Assad’s Syrian army units fleeing the country and others switching allegiance to the new Government, Israel has stepped in, issuing ultimatums for groups in the Yarmouk Basin to surrender all weapons, submit to home searches, and evacuate their villages or face military action. This has forced many families to evacuate their homes. Israeli officials claim the move is necessary to prevent armed groups from building up near their border. If the transitional Government fails to gain control, Israel is likely to deepen its presence, expanding the buffer zone under the pretext of counterterrorism. So far, the transitional Government has not taken any steps to oppose Israel’s expansion in southern Syria.
The IDF could move far beyond the initial 15km buffer zone towards the Damascus–Al Sweida highway, aiming to secure most of Quneitra and Dar’a and parts of Al Sweida. Syrian factions, including armed groups affiliated with the transitional Government, might try to stop the advance, though their capacity to pose a sustained military threat remains limited owing to fragmentation, resource constraints, and a lack of advanced weaponry. There is also a low to medium likelihood of Iran and Hezbollah reopening fronts in Lebanon or southern Syria to slow Israeli gains. The probability of large-scale retaliation remains moderate to low, and isolated attacks or proxy activity are more likely.
The continued absence of the transitional Government in these areas, its inability to counter Israeli expansion, and failure to protect civilians are likely to fuel further tensions and protests similar to the ones that erupted in Al Sweida in April 2025 against Israel and the Government’s failure to protect civilians. Between 8 December 2024 and 12 June 2025, Israeli attacks killed at least 22 civilians in Al Sweida, Dar’a, Quneitra, and Rural Damascus. ([ACAPS 22/07/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))
Hazard materialisation: The hazard partially materialised. Israel continued to expand and consolidate its military presence in southern Syria through repeated ground incursions, arrests, checkpoints, civilian property destruction, and movement restrictions, particularly across Quneitra and western Dar’a governorates. Israeli forces established additional military positions and normalised near-daily operations inside Syrian territory, while protests against the continued military presence increased from June–July 2026, reflecting growing civilian resentment. Israel also continued to justify its operations on security grounds and the protection of Druze communities. That said, the risk overestimated the likelihood that Israeli expansion would trigger sustained armed resistance by Syrian factions or Iran-backed groups. Instead, opposition remained largely limited to local protests and isolated confrontations, while the transitional Government continued to avoid direct military confrontation with Israel. Likewise, Israeli operations did not expand into the broader territorial advance towards As Sweida or the Damascus–As Sweida highway suggested in the risk.

Risk Title: A prolonged Syria–Lebanon border conflict results in displacement and increases shelter and livelihood needs
Rationale:
The Syria–Lebanon border remains a key smuggling corridor for fuel, drugs (especially Captagon), and weapons, primarily from Syria to Lebanon, often facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. After Al Assad’s fall, Syria’s transitional Government’s forces launched an anti-smuggling campaign in early 2025, targeting routes used by Hezbollah-linked clans near Al Qasr village on the Lebanese side of the border. Armed networks, such as the Jaafar clan (of Lebanon), resisted violently, ambushing Syrian patrols and firing anti-tank rockets. These confrontations escalated into clashes in March near Al Qasr.
Without clear coordination between Lebanese and Syrian authorities, both aiming to stop smuggling, efforts to dismantle these networks will likely trigger more cross-border skirmishes, especially in areas where smuggling remains a main source of income and power for local armed groups.
On 16 March 2025, clashes broke out along the Syria–Lebanon border after transitional Government soldiers crossed into Lebanon and were shot by local Lebanese clans. Syria’s transitional Government accused Hezbollah of abducting and executing three of its soldiers, which Hezbollah denied. In response, Syrian troops shelled Lebanese border villages, killing civilians and triggering counterfire from local clans and the Lebanese Army. The two days of fighting killed at least ten people, including a 15-year-old boy, and wounded over 50 in Al Qasr. The two Governments reached a ceasefire on 17 March, ending the clashes.
Areas including Al Qasr have served as hubs for Iranian weapon transfers, protected by clan networks aligned with Hezbollah. Another factor driving tensions between Syria and Lebanon is, in fact, Hezbollah’s presence along Lebanon’s northeast border and its ties to local Shia clans and longstanding smuggling routes from Syria. Syria’s new transitional Government sees these ties as a security threat and has targeted Shia-populated border zones, shelling villages and expelling Lebanese Shia families. Hezbollah has avoided direct clashes with Syria’s transitional Government so far, but tensions have been rising between the two parties and within Lebanon, between Hezbollah and the Lebanese Government. When Lebanese forces seized Hezbollah weapons in April, local supporters of the party and armed groups accused the Lebanese army of betraying them for cooperating with Syria.
If crackdowns on smuggling continue and Hezbollah and drug-smuggling criminal groups see their supply routes further threatened, localised armed confrontations along the border also have the potential to turn into broader fighting. Syrian forces already advanced up to 5–7km into Lebanese territory around Al Qasr in March to dismantle smuggling routes, and further incursions to similarly shallow depths — meaning within the 5–7km border zone — remain possible, though recent diplomatic talks between the Governments of Lebanon and Syria in April and the creation of a joint border committee may reduce the likelihood of a sustained escalation. The committee, established as part of a bilateral border agreement, is a ministerial-level body tasked with coordinating border management, preventing unauthorised crossings, and overseeing dispute resolution in sensitive areas.
Although Syrian forces have imposed military control over the border with Lebanon, challenges such as difficult terrain, Hezbollah’s presence, and some southern clans’ reliance on smuggling continue to threaten lasting border security. These factors may enable smuggling networks to regroup, casting doubt on Syria’s capacity for sustained and effective border monitoring. Hezbollah could respond militarily to any advance of Syrian troops, not only to defend strategic smuggling routes that sustain its operations but also to assert its role as a protector of Lebanese sovereignty and maintain influence in border areas with high Shia presence. That said, considering the conflict between Hezbollah and Israel between October 2023 and November 2024, which significantly weakened Hezbollah’s military capacity, the likelihood of its direct engagement remains between medium to low.
Given its limited capacity and history of constrained responses, including during recent Israeli operations, the Lebanese Army is unlikely to play a decisive role but may be drawn into localised clashes. On the other hand, Syrian Sunni armed groups could exploit the instability to target Lebanese and Syrian Shia communities in border areas, driven by sectarian tensions and perceptions of Hezbollah’s alignment with Al Assad’s rule, further escalating the violence. Although the likelihood of escalating tensions and an advance by the new Syrian army remains moderate, the consequences could include a prolonged border conflict, mass displacement, and rising casualties on both sides. [(ACAPS 22/07/2025)](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

Risk Title: Severe shortage of services triggers unrest and breakout attempts in Al Hol and Al Roj camps
Rationale:
If security in Al Hol and Al Roj camps collapses due to mass rioting or breakouts, ISIS-affiliated IDPs are likely to escape, regroup, and rejoin IS cells, potentially sparking renewed insurgencies in both Syria and Iraq. Unlike typical displacement sites, Al Hol and Al Roj function as detention facilities housing individuals with suspected IS ties, including non-Syrians and their families, making the risk of escape a security concern rather than a humanitarian one. As of April 2024, Al Hol hosts 42,000 people, and as of December 2024 Al Roj hosts over 2,600 people. As of early April, around 1,500 international troops remain in Syria, some of whom are tasked with preventing an IS resurgence; large-scale escapes could prompt renewed military operations in Syria. Iraqi officials have repeatedly warned that instability in Al Hol poses a direct threat to their internal security, as escaped IS members may attempt to cross into Iraq. Compounding this risk, a recent US funding freeze has weakened camp management, including WASH services, and could create further security vacuums that IS may exploit.
In January 2025, President Trump’s administration ordered a temporary freeze on nearly all US foreign aid, including humanitarian assistance. This affected funding to support humanitarian programmes and aid delivery in northeastern Syria. Aid and service delivery in Al Hol camp and Al Roj camp, hosting people displaced from areas previously under the control of the IS in Syria, had relied heavily on USAID support. Risk Title: Water scarcity, especially in northeast and northwest Syria result in livelihoods and services’ disruptions, reduced food production and protests
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
As of February 2025, about 13.6 million Syrians lack access to safe water and sanitation. Conflict since 2011 has damaged water infrastructure, resulting in a 40% reduction in the drinking water supply as of 2021. Almost half of the water systems no longer function reliably, forcing many to rely on tankers or unsafe wells. Ongoing electricity and fuel shortages have crippled water pumps and treatment plants, exacerbating water rationing and existing sanitation problems and driving disease outbreaks. 
Syria and the region experienced an exceptionally dry winter and spring in 2024/2025, with significantly below-average rainfall and higher temperatures. In April 2025, water levels in Lake Euphrates Dam dropped to about six meters, which is five meters below the normal level.
Upstream water retention and weaponisation of water are also drivers of water scarcity in Syria. Türkiye has sharply reduced the Euphrates’ waters flow into Syria by restricting releases from upstream dams, such as the Atatürk Dam, often to around 200 cubic meters per second, well below the 500 cubic meters per second agreed in bilateral treaties. It has also used dam releases as political leverage and targeted key water infrastructure like the Alouk station in Al Hasakah in August 2024 and October 2023, disrupting access to water for more than a million people. Similarly, Israel’s occupation of the Golan Heights since 1981 and control over the Yarmouk basin and Unity (Al Wahda) dam in December 2024 have cut Syria off from its southern water sources. Communities, especially agricultural, living in southern Syria are likely to experience the impact of the loss of these water sources throughout 2025.
The lean season in Syria typically runs from June to September. In 2025, it will likely be one of the driest since 1989. April forecasts showed poor soil moisture and low reservoir levels heading into summer. As rainfall was far below average during the October–April season, water scarcity will likely intensify through June to September. Water levels are likely to continue to decrease in 2025, as projections indicate that by 2050, Syria’s water supply will decrease by 20%.
Water-related tensions have driven protests and localised disputes before, and are likely to drive further protests and disputes in 2025. In June 2024, water shortages and electricity cuts led to localised protests in Al Hasakeh. In February 2024, residents in Deir ez-Zor protested over lack of drinking water and accused local officials of corruption. In July 2022, displaced people in several camps in north Idlib protested water shortages, while water service providers went on a strike to protest an international organisation's decision to reduce water supplies.
Northeast and Northwest Syria, particularly Al Hasakeh, Al Raqqa, Idlib, and rural Aleppo, are likely hotspots for water-related tensions during the 2025 lean season. People’s livelihoods in these areas are already the most impacted by water scarcity, and they have limited alternative sources. If shortages persist, it is likely that people will protest at wells or water trucks, attempt to blockade water pipelines, or engage in local skirmishes over water resources. For example, communities might block a contested pump station or forcibly redirect tanker convoys. ([ECHO 19/06/2024](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syria-historic-drought-impacting-food-security-dg-echo-un-ocha-fao-wfp-echo-daily-flash-19-june-2025), [FAO accessed12/09/2025](https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/bf52f354-c8f3-4f3f-9367-4d5347016c7b), [UNICEF accessed 12/09/2025](https://www.unicef.org/syria/situation-children-syria), [CSIC accessed 12/09/2025](https://features.csis.org/the-future-of-the-Euphrates-River/), [Ul 03/05/2025](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com))
