The risk has slightly improved because above-average rainfall in February and March 2026 provided some short-term relief to water availability in parts of Syria. However, structural drivers of water scarcity remain in place, including damaged water infrastructure, limited pumping and treatment capacity, and the long-term effects of climate change. At the same time, several flooding events affected Al Hasakah, Ar Raqqa, and Deir ez Zor governorates, impacting an estimated 6,000 people in March. Additional heavy rainfall affected approximately 19,000 people in Aleppo and Idlib governorates. While the rainfall may temporarily improve water availability and soil moisture in some areas, flooding has also damaged crops, agricultural land, and infrastructure, potentially reducing food production and access to food for affected communities.

UPDATE 12/02/2026
Water scarcity has intensified since December 2025, with catastrophic agricultural impacts. Wheat production has falled by over 50% compared to pre-war norms, while barley production has dropped by 65% below the five-year average as a result of drought, extreme heat, insecurity, and high input costs. Agricultural drought models indicate over 700,000 hectares in central and northern Syria will face drought between January–March 2026, with Aleppo, Al Hasakeh, Ar Raqqa, Hama, and Idleb governorates worst affected. In early February, flash floods in Idleb and Lattakia killed at least two children and inundated displacement camps. While rainfall is desperately needed, intense storms risk washing away fertile topsoil rather than replenishing reservoirs. During January clashes, residents in Aleppo and Al Hasakeh experienced days without water after authorities took control of Tishreen Dam. The transitional Government's northeast takeover has transferred water management from Kurdish-led authorities to Damascus. Damascus has reaffirmed commitments to share 58% of Euphrates flows with Iraq and announced multilevel water governance reforms, though implementation details remain pending.

Risk Title: Renewed violence in As Sweida or settler outpost establishment drives Israeli expansion in southern Syria, displacing civilians and restricting access
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
Since the fall of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024, Israel’s military presence in southern Syria has evolved from incursions into sustained territorial control. By early 2026, Israeli forces have expanded beyond the UN-monitored 1974 separation line into parts of Quneitra and western Dar’a, establishing military posts, outposts, and checkpoints. By mid-2026, the presence had become increasingly entrenched, with regular patrols and ground activity beyond the former separation area. Further expansion of positions, checkpoints, or closed military zones would indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. Sustained territorial control or restrictions on civilian access could increase local resistance and create conditions for further expansion towards areas linked to As Sweida.
Two pathways could accelerate or formalise this existing trajectory in the next three to six months. One is the revival of a proposal for a humanitarian corridor, first suggested in 2025 by Israeli officials to provide aid for Druze in As Sweida, particularly if renewed violence in As Sweida gives Israel a justification to intervene on behalf of the Druze and expand in southern Syria. The proposed corridor would connect the governorate with the Golan area, including Hader near Mount Hermon and Druze villages along the Syrian Golan. Although the proposal was previously rejected by the Syrian transitional Government, renewed violence or deterioration in As Sweida could bring it back into discussions and provide a pretext for expanding Israeli control or establishing protected access through southern Syria. While Israel framed its military intervention during the July 2025 violence as protecting the Druze, Druze opinion remains divided. One senior spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, has welcomed Israeli involvement, while the other two have consistently rejected foreign interference, and As Sweida's Druze security chief warned it had complicated reconciliation.
A second pathway is the activity of Israeli settlers seeking to establish a permanent presence. The Pioneers of Bashan,  an Israeli settler movement, have repeatedly attempted to cross into southern Syria and establish outposts, including around Hader and Mount Hermon, with their stated ambitions extending across As Sweida, Dar'a, and Quneitra governorates. More than 40 settlers entered the outskirts of Hader in April, while approximately 70–100 attempted to cross through Mount Hermon in July, followed by further attempts in August. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data indicates an upward trend in incursion attempts since April 2026, peaking sharply in July with six recorded events. Although the Israel Defense Forces have so far prevented permanent settlement, repeated attempts could increase pressure on Israeli authorities to eventually formalise such activity.
If either pathway materialises, further Israeli control and presence in southern Syria are likely to restrict civilian movement and access to agricultural land through additional checkpoints, patrols, and military restrictions. An expanded Israeli presence could also prompt resistance from Syrian government forces, as well as communities or armed groups in Quneitra and western Dar'a, increasing the probability of clashes around Israeli positions. Current vulnerability / Coping capacitie:
There are already 1.37 million people in need in the three governorates exposed to Israeli expansion in southern Syria, including 872,200 in Dar’a, 384,000 in As Sweida, and 110,500 in Quneitra. 
In western Dar’a, Israeli military activity, movement restrictions and explosive ordnance contamination have restricted access to farmland and grazing areas and disrupted agricultural livelihoods. By June 2026, more than 32,000 returnees had been recorded in western Dar’a since December 2024, adding pressure to already-overstretched health, water, and education services. In Quneitra and Dar’a, Israeli forces carried out incursions, shelled farmland, and detained civilians through July 2026, restricting access to land and reducing household income. In As Sweida, 32% of assessed communities in May were facing multiple severe needs, mainly related to livelihoods, health, and protection. Renewed insecurity and armed clashes further disrupt livelihoods and access to essential services.
Coping capacity is weakened by limited livelihood opportunities and gaps in humanitarian assistance. By 24 August, 83% of assessed locations in As Sweida reported challenges to the reintegration of displaced people, while limited employment opportunities and depleted savings are constraining households’ ability to meet basic needs. Humanitarian assistance also faces funding constraints, with WFP suspending assistance for more than 72,000 IDPs across As Sweida, Quneitra, and Rural Damascus since the end of July 2026. Expected impact:
If the risk materialises, As Sweida, Dar’a, and Quneitra governorates are expected to face increased displacement, agricultural and livestock livelihood losses, deteriorating food access, and further disruption to water and essential services.
Further Israeli restrictions on farmland and grazing areas would reduce household income and food production. Between 70–80% of communities in southern Syria are dependent on farming for food, but Quneitra households in the immediate border zone have already reduced crop production because of Israeli military operations, further contributing to deteriorating food insecurity. In Dar’a, further restrictions on agricultural land could reduce household income during a critical period for potato and tomato production, with above-average 2026 harvests already generating limited returns because of weak prices and high input costs. Israeli incursions in July also cut agricultural labourers, herders, and farming households off from farmland and grazing areas during the harvest season, reducing cash income.
Expansion of Israeli positions or clashes around outposts and a protected corridor could trigger new displacement, particularly from communities surrounding Israeli positions. As Sweida is particularly exposed, with around 101,000 people internally displaced there by April 2026, equivalent to 21% of its population, while previous violence has displaced thousands towards Dar’a. Further displacement would increase pressure on host communities and already-strained services in Dar’a and As Sweida.
Further Israeli expansion could disrupt access to water infrastructure and sources in western Dar’a villages, particularly around new military positions or along a protected corridor. In Maariya, Israeli military activity around the site between May–June led to the sabotage of the village well, leaving residents dependent on costly private water supplies. In Abdin, piped water has been unavailable for a second consecutive year, with households paying around SYP 150,000 (USD 11.50) per tanker, while critically low water levels in Abdin Dam are already threatening irrigation in the Yarmuk Basin. Further Israeli expansion around these water sources could compound existing shortages, increase household water costs, and disrupt agricultural production.
Men in areas that may be affected by Israeli incursions could face increased protection risks from detention, interrogation, and movement restrictions. Israeli forces have continued to temporarily detain Syrian men during raids and at checkpoints, with some released after hours of questioning, while others have been transferred to Israeli detention facilities for months without publicly stated grounds. By 17 August, Israeli forces were still detaining at least 47 Syrians after the release of over 140 in July.

Risk Title: Flooding and landslides in Tanzania kill people, destroy infrastructure, damage crops, and increase waterborne diseases, aggravating socioeconomic and environmental vulnerabilities
Rationale:
Since 2010, the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in Tanzania have increased, including heavy rainfall, flooding, and landslides. These events pose a significant threat to people’s lives, basic infrastructure, food security, and public health. According to Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts for February–April 2025, several regions will experience above-average rainfall, which could heighten existing vulnerabilities, such as weak infrastructure, poor waste management, and unsustainable land use.
Past floods in Kilimanjaro, Kilombero, Manyara, Mbeya, Morogoro, and Rufiji regions have had significant humanitarian and socioeconomic impacts, including loss of life, property destruction, displacement, and economic decline. Crop damage poses a serious threat to livelihoods, and stagnant floodwaters increase the spread of waterborne diseases such as cholera and malaria. The lack of effective disaster preparedness and response mechanisms further aggravate the crisis, leaving affected populations with limited coping capacity.
Hazard materialisation: The Tanzania Meteorological Authority's ten-day forecast for 21–31 March 2025 accurately predicted the occurrence of heavy thundershowers and strong winds in specific areas. This forecast materialised between 21–24 March, as continuous heavy rainfall accompanied by strong winds affected Ulanga district in Morogoro region and a prolonged thunderstorm with heavy rainfall and strong winds affected Musoma municipality and surrounding areas in Mara region. These weather events, characterised by their intensity and duration, represent the materialised hazard that was anticipated by the meteorological forecasts for these locations during that time frame.

Risk Title: Drought conditions due to the El Nino, high rice prices in the international market, and restrictions imposed by India on their rice exports worsen food insecurity outcomes
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
RATIONALE AND IMPACT
Timor-Leste has around 262,000 people facing high acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) as per IPC projections for May - September 2023. The food insecurity situation will be worsened due to certain environmental and economic factors. Drought conditions due to the El Nino, high rice prices in the international market, and restrictions imposed by India on their rice exports worsen food insecurity outcomes

The entire country of Timor-Leste is showing signs of drought due to the ongoing El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) conditions and is forecasted to strengthen and persist until early 2024. Prolonged dry spells will negatively impact agriculture output in the country. The agriculture sector accounts for around 27% (around 63,000) of total employment. Outside of the labour force, around 162,000 people are subsistence foodstuff producers. 

The international rice prices surged between July and September 2023, which raised the costs of rice within Timor-Leste and the retail prices of imported rice in the country. The surge in rice prices have made it unaffordable for impoverished families in Timor-Leste. People in the country depend heavily on imports of rice, especially imported Indian rice which comprise around 90% of rice imports by Timor-Leste. The Indian government introduced measures aimed at stabilising domestic food prices which included a ban on exports of non-basmati white rice, 20% export duty on non-basmati parboiled rice, and the imposition of a minimum export price. These measures are aggravating the already worsened rice availability and subsequently consumption situation in Timor-Leste. 

Current stock of rice may only cover just over one month of national rice consumption needs. If the country is unable to secure enough rice and nutritious food as soon as possible, there will be further deterioration of the nutritional and food security status among the poorest and most vulnerable Timorese families. 

AGGRAVATING FACTORS
Oil and gas are the main export products in the fuel and mining products category. In 2022, fuel and mining products contributed to more than 80% of total exports. It also contributes to around 70% of total government revenues. Timor-Leste’s real GDP is estimated to fall by around 17% in 2023, primarily due to reduced oil and gas production.  The real GDP is expected to decline by 6% in 2024. The current and short-term economic situation will reduce livelihood opportunities, aggravating the food insecurity situation in the country.
Hazard materialisation:
Poverty, El Nino induced drought-like conditions, and high food prices were found to be among the primary drivers of food insecurity.

Unfavourable weather conditions including the current El Nino event, and shortfall in production of rice in the main rice producing and exporting countries, led to limited global rice availability.

Rice and maize are the two main staple foods in the country. Timor-Leste has high dependency on imported rice to meet their demand of rice. Price of imported rice was 30% higher in December 2023 compared to December 2022. Maize prices rose by 66% during the same period, and its production is expected to decrease in 2024 due to the impact of El Nino and fall armyworm infestations.

Risk Title: Protests against agricultural exports from Ukraine intensify across the European Union block Ukraine’s border leading to further economic strain.
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
Prior to 2022, 90% of all exports from Ukraine were via its Black Sea ports, with the remaining 10% via land. Additionally, all seaports in Crimea have been under Russian occupation since 2014. In February 2022, Russia started a full-scale invasion against Ukraine and a sea blockade. 

In May 2022, the European Commission established alternative 'Solidarity Lanes', which are alternative export routes through the EU to support Ukraine. The Solidarity Lanes have enabled the export of around 60% of Ukraine's grain since 2022. The Grain deal reached in July 2022 also supported Ukraine's sea exports until Russia withdrew from it in July 2023. Although Ukraine managed to resume sea exports by targeting the Russian navy, it still depends on EU Solidarity Lanes. 

Farmers across EU are protesting against rising costs and taxes, environmental rules and competition from lower cost food imports. In Poland, protestors have been blocking Ukrainian agricultural products from transiting. 

The additional strain on Ukraine's economy that is already affected by war could increase as more EU farmers join the blockade of Ukraine's border with the EU. As sociopolitical tensions increase, the blockade could start affecting the movement of civilians and other goods, as well as humanitarian and defense related movements of goods and personnel. 

UPDATE 28 February 2024

According to media reports as at 28 February 2024, Poland is planning a temporary closure of the border with Ukraine, including the exchange of goods. The stated aim by Poland is to protect its market, despite Poland's ban on grain from Ukraine. This developing situation will likely lead to trade between Poland and Ukraine being affected. On 20 March, media reported a blockade at Medyka-Shehyni cross point for transportation buses for civilians traveling to and from Ukraine. On the same day, mass protests took place across Poland, with police estimating blockades in 570 locations, including against access into major cities and the capital Warsaw.

In reaction, Ukraine started planning to increase the use of the Danube River export route to avoid the potential Polish border blockade despite the ongoing risk of Russian attacks on Ukraine's ports and export infrastructure.

On 25 February 2024, there was a sabotage attack that resulted in spilling of 160 tons of grain from Ukraine transiting by railway through Poland to other countries. Prior to this incident, there were several small-scale incidents in which grain was deliberately spilled by protestors in Poland, with no suspects detained. The sabotage of grain and the usage of anti-Ukrainian slogans by some protestors in Poland increased tensions between Ukraine and Poland. 

UPDATE 30/03/2024

On 7 March, according to protest organisers 150,000 people took to the streets, while official figures stated there were 30,000 people.

On 20 March 2024, there were also country wide protests with 70,000 protestors, and 570 or 580 blockades in major cities including the capital Warsaw, as well as on the border with Ukraine where Polish protesters restricted the passage of buses transferring travellers at the Medyka-Shehyni crossing according to Ukraine's Border Guard Service, in addition to the movement of trucks with goods.

UPDATE 29/04/2024
Polish farmers suspended the blockades and protests on the border with Ukraine in late April 2024 after the Polish government decided to pay subsidies to the farmers, however there is yet some uncertainty whether the suspension would last.

Risk Type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
Rationale:
On 25 March 2025, the new US administration – under President Donald Trump – reached an agreement with Ukraine and Russia on a temporary 30-day pause in attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukraine agreed with the US on a list of energy facilities that Russia should stop attacking, although Russia took some oil and gas production facilities off the list and has continued attacking them.

Given the history of Russian forces violating ceasefire agreements since 2014, they are likely to also violate this agreement and resort to disinformation and false flag attacks to conceal the violations, possibly blaming Ukraine for disrupting the ceasefire agreement. In this context, US officials may downplay these violations to claim the success of the US-led ceasefire.
Russian forces, having stockpiled missiles and drones for use against the energy sector, may step up their attacks on civilian infrastructure, such as residential areas, as a sustained political tactic especially following the US-led negotiations for a full ceasefire. A recent such attack was on 4 April, which targeted a residential area in Kryvyi Rih city, Dnipropetrovska, killing 19 people (including 9 children). Alternatively, Russian forces could accumulate the missiles and drones that they planned to use in 2024 then launch a major countrywide combined missile and drone attack against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure immediately after the partial ceasefire ends in late April while also stalling negotiations. ([ACAPS 13/09/2024](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20240913_ACAPS_Ukraine_Analysis_hub_Attacks_on_the_energy_infrastructure_in_Ukraine.pdf), [ACAPS 12/02/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250219_ACAPS_Ukraine_-_Energy_infrastructure_attacks-_Updated_outlook_and_impact_during_the_2024-2025_cold_season_.pdf), [Dixigroup 31/03/2025](https://dixigroup.org/en/analytic/russian-war-against-ukraine-energy-dimension-dixi-group-alert-weekly-review-93/), [Kyiv Independent 03/04/2025](https://kyivindependent.com/ukraine-informs-us-about-russias-energy-ceasefire-violations/))
Hazard materialisation:
The risk of large-scale civilian harm in Ukraine is steadily materialising as Russian forces intensify attacks on densely populated areas and critical infrastructure alongside US-led peace negotiations. Civilians have born the brunt of these hostilities, with repeated missile and drone strikes since April 2025 causing mass casualties, widespread destruction, and compounding humanitarian vulnerabilities.
Throughout April 2025, ballistic and aerial strikes frequently targeted residential areas, leading to exceptionally high civilian casualties, including a significant number of children, and marking one of the deadliest months since the escalation of the conflict. Notably, a wave of coordinated attacks on 24 April struck multiple oblasts across the country, inflicting dozens of deaths and hundreds of injuries while devastating residential structures and essential infrastructure. This surge coincided with heightened ceasefire diplomacy, suggesting that military escalation may have accompanied negotiations. Data collected during this period points to an overall rise in damage to civilian infrastructure compared with previous months.
A second escalation phase unfolded in May, characterised by consecutive nationwide strikes coinciding with a major prisoner exchange, the largest since 2014. Despite agreements for regular exchanges having been brokered in advance, the timing reinforces the pattern of intensified attacks during politically significant moments, including foreign-mediated talks. This trend persisted into June, when Russia markedly shifted focus to energy networks and agricultural sites. Critical infrastructure in Khersonska and Poltavska oblasts was severely damaged, while high-precision missile strikes on Kyiv and Odeska oblasts repeatedly struck residential buildings and even medical facilities. A missile strike on Dnipro on 24 June alone caused over 300 civilian casualties, underlining the increasingly indiscriminate and destructive nature of the campaign. By the end of that month, the sustained targeting of energy facilities led to rolling blackouts that deepened civilian hardship.
The scale of attacks further intensified during July. Mass strikes employing hundreds of drones and missiles repeatedly targeted Kyiv and other urban centres, with devastating consequences for civilians. Attacks directly striking residential buildings in Kharkivska and Kyiv oblasts resulted in dozens to more than a hundred casualties in a single incident. These escalations repeatedly coincided with milestones in US-led negotiations, including the Istanbul talks and public statements from US officials warning of sanction deadlines, reinforcing the link between diplomatic events and heightened violence.
In late August, the attacks reached unprecedented levels, with Russian forces deploying hundreds of drones and dozens of missiles in a single day. High-precision strikes on Kyiv oblast killed and injured many civilians, while attacks on energy and gas infrastructure in multiple oblasts left over 100,000 people without power. The systematic targeting of both residential and critical infrastructure confirmed the sustained strategy of leveraging military pressure to influence negotiation dynamics while maximising civilian suffering.
Taken together, this sustained campaign has transformed from a succession of isolated strikes into a persistent pattern of large-scale hostilities against civilians and essential services. The increasing frequency, geographic spread, and strategic timing of the attacks, particularly around peace negotiations and prisoner exchanges, demonstrate a deliberate escalation strategy. This materialisation of risk is evidenced by rising casualty figures, compounded infrastructure damage, and growing humanitarian consequences for millions of civilians caught between military offensives and the fragile negotiation process. Risk Title: The US–Iran escalation leads to strikes on Houthi-held ports, crippling infrastructure and disrupting vital humanitarian supply chains in Yemen
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
The de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) have pledged to respond to any US attack against Iran in early 2026, most likely by escalating Red Sea maritime attacks and launching direct strikes against Israel and US military bases in the region. By 19 February 2026, this risk had become imminent following a ten-day ultimatum issued by the US Administration for Iran to reach a nuclear and regional agreement, placing a potential military trigger in late February or early March. Any Houthi retaliatory attack would likely invite a renewed, intensified US or Israeli air campaign against Houthi military and economic infrastructure, with ports and other critical civilian infrastructure among the most likely targets.
Previous rounds of strikes have demonstrated the severe humanitarian consequences of this pattern. Israeli strikes on Sana’a between August–September 2025 killed at least 45 people and wounded over 230 others across multiple incidents, with residential areas, a fuel station supplying hospitals, and media offices among the sites struck. Al Hodeidah port – through which approximately 70% of Yemen's commercial imports and 80% of its humanitarian assistance pass – has been repeatedly targeted, with its operational capacity severely degraded. This infrastructure damage is compounded by access constraints stemming from the DFA's targeting of humanitarian organisations. The DFA has increasingly accused humanitarian responders of criminality, raided UN compounds, detained staff, and levelled accusations of espionage against aid workers. These raids and detentions have a cooling effect on NGOs working in DFA-controlled areas, with organisations reducing staffing to 'essential levels' and lowering operational risk thresholds, leading to reduced programming or withdrawal.
The WFP’s January 2026 decision to shut down operations and lay off all 365 staff in northern Yemen exemplifies this compounding effect, leaving 18 million people without humanitarian aid. This, alongside restrictions and the targeting of UN bodies and INGOs by the DFA, means the transfer of risks to grassroots organisations, which often serve as the first and sometimes only responders in remote areas.
